div.head: CHAP. 3.
Of mariedMarriedmarried folkesFolksfolks.
div.p: A Familiefamily is distinguished into sundry combinations or couples of persons.

A couple, is that wherbywhereby two persons standing in mutuallmutual relation to each other, are combined together as it were in one. And of these two, the one is alwaiesalways higher, and beareth rule, the other is lower, and yeeldethyieldeth subiectionsubjection.
Couples are of two sorts; principallprincipal, or lesseless principallprincipal.
The principallprincipal, is the combination of mariedmarried folkesfolks; and these are so termed in respect of Mariagemarriage.

MariageMarriage is the lawfulllawful coniunctionconjunction of the two mariedmarried persons; that is, of one man, and one woman into one flesh. So was the first institution of mariagemarriage, Gen. 2. 21. whichWhich is expounded by our SauiourSaviour Christ, Matth. 19. 6. TherforeTherefore they are no more two, but one flesh. And also by Paul, Ephes. 5. 31. For this cause shall a man leaueleave father and mother, and shall

Wherefore this is an eternal law of mariagemarriage, that two, and not three or fourefour, shall be one flesh. And for this cause, the fathers, who had many wiueswives and
Concubines, it may be that through customecustom they sinned of ignorance, yet they are not in any wise to be excused.

MariageMarriage of it selfeself is a thing indifferent, and the kingdomekingdom of God stands no more in it, then in meats and drinks; and yet it is a state in it selfeself, farrefar more excellent, then the condition of single life. For first, it was ordained by God in Paradise, aboueabove and before all other states of life, in Adams innocencieinnocency before the fall. AgaineAgain, it was instituted vponupon a most serious and solemnesolemn consultation among the three persons in the holy TrinitieTrinity. Genes. 1. 26. Let vsus make man in our image, according to our likenesselikeness, and let them rule ouerover, &c. Gen. 2. 18. IehouahJehovah Elohim said, It is not good that the man should be himselfehimself alone, I will make him an helpehelp meetemeet for him. Thirdly, the manner of this coniunctionconjunction was excellent, for God ioynedjoined our first parents Adam and EueEve together immediately. Fourthly, God gauegave a large blessing vntounto the estate of mariagemarriage, saying, Increase and multipliemultiply and fill the earth. Lastly, mariagemarriage was made & appointed
by God himselfehimself, to be the fountainefountain and seminarieseminary of all other sorts & kinds of life, in the Commoncommon-wealth and in the Church.

Now if mankind had continued in that vprightnesuprightness and integritieintegrity which it had by creation, the state of single life had been of no price and estimation amongst men, neither should it hauehave had any place in the world, without great contempt of Gods ordinance and blessing.

NeuerthelesseNevertheless, since the fall, to some men who hauehave the gift of continenciecontinency, it is in many respects farrefar better then mariagemarriage, yet not simpliesimply, but only by accident, in regard of sundriesundry calamities which came into the world by sin. For, first it freeth a man from many and great cares of housholdhousehold affairesaffairs. AgaineAgain, it maketh him much more fit & disposed to meditate of heauenlyheavenly things, without distraction of mind. Besides that, when dangers are either present, or imminent, in matters belonging to this life, the single person is in this case happiehappy, because he and his are more secure
and safe, then others be who are in mariedmarried state. 1. Cor. 7. 8. Therefore I say to the vnmariedunmarried and widoweswidows, It is good for them if they abide eueneven as I do. vers. 26. I suppose then this to be good for the present necessitienecessity, I meanemean, that it is good for a man so to be, vers. 28. But if thou takest a wife thou sinnest not, and if a virgin marriemarry she sinneth not; neuerthelessenevertheless such shall hauehave trouble in the flesh, vers. 32. And I would hauehave you without care.
The end of mariagemarriage is fourefoldfourfold.

The first is, procreation of children, for the propagation and continuance of the seed and posteritieposterity of man vponupon the earth, Gen. 1. 28. BringforthBring forth fruit multipliemultiply, fill the earth, and subdue it, Genes. 9. 1. 1. Tim. 5. 14.

The second is the procreation of an holy seed, wherbywhereby the Church of God may be kept holy and chaste, and there may alwaiesalways be a holy company of men, that may worship and serueserve God in the Church from age to age, Malach. 2. 15. And did not he make one? yetYet had heehe abundance of spirit; and wherefore one? becauseBecause he sought a godly seed.

The third is, that after the fall of mankind, it might be a soueraignesovereign meanesmeans to auoidavoid fornication, and consequently to subdue and slake the burning lusts of the flesh, 1. Cor. 7. 2. NeuerthelesseNevertheless for the auoidingavoiding of fornication, let eueryevery man hauehave his wife, and eueryevery woman hauehave her husband. vers. 9. But if they cannot abstaineabstain, let them marriemarry; for it is better to marriemarry, then to burneburn. And for this cause, some SchoolemenSchoolmen doedo erreerr, who hold that the secret commingcoming together of man and wife, cannot be without sinnesin, vnlesseunless it be done for procreation of children. Lombard the master of the Sentences saith the contrariecontrary, namely, that mariagemarriage before the fall was only a dutieduty, but now since the fall it is also remedieremedy.

The fourth end is, that the parties married may thereby performeperform the duties of their callings, in better and more comfortable manner. ProuProv. 31. 11. The heart of her husband trusteth her, and heehe shall hauehave no need of spoilespoil. vers. 13. She seeketh woollwool, and flaxeflax, and laboureth cheerefullycheerfully with her hands.

MariageMarriage is free to alall orders, and sorts
of men without exception, eueneven to those that hauehave the gift of contimenciecontinency; but for them which cannot abstaineabstain, it i • s, by the expresseexpress commandementcommandment of God, necessarienecessary. By which it appeareth to be a cleareclear case, that the commandementcommandment of the Pope of Rome, whereby he forbiddeth mariagemarriage of certainecertain persons, as namely, of ClergieClergy men, is meerelymerely diabolicalldiabolical; for so writeth the Apostle, 1. But against this doctrine sundriesundry things are alleagedalleged.

ObiectObject. 1. The Apostle commandeth the married among the CorinthesCorinthians, to abstaineabstain with consent for a time, that they might giuegive themseluesthemselves to fasting and praierprayer, 1. Cor. 7. 5. I answereanswer, that Paul speakesspeaks not in that place of daily and common

By the first faith, Paul vnderstandethunderstandeth that promise and vow which they made vntounto Christ, when they were baptised; and they are there said to begin to waxewax wanton against Christ, by denying or renouncing that faith, and not otherwise.
ObiectObject. 4. He that doth earnestly and from his heart, crauecrave the gift of continenciecontinency, God will giuegive it him, and therforetherefore he need not marriemarry.

div.head: CHAP. 4.
Of the Contract.
div.p: MArriageMarriage hath two distinct parts, the first is the beginning; the second, the accomplishment or consummation thereof.

The Beginning, is the Contractcontract or Espousals; the End or accomplishmētaccomplishment, is the solemnesolemn Manifestation of the Contractcontract, by that which properly we call Mariagemarriage. Deut. 20. 7. What man is there that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her? Let him go and returnereturn againeagain vntounto his house, lest he die in battellbattle, and another man take her. Matth. 1. 18. When his mother MarieMary was betrothed to IosephJoseph, before they came together, She was found with child of the Holy Ghost.
BetweeneBetween the Contractcontract and Marriagemarriage, there ought to beebe some certainecertain space or distance of time. The reasons whereof may be these:

First, a businessebusiness of so great importance as this is, would not be rashly or
vnaduisedlyunadvisedly attempted, but should rather be done by degrees in processeprocess of time, according to that saying, not so ancient as true.Diu deliberandum quod se • mel stat • uendum. Actions of weight, before resolution, require mature deliberation, Secondly, That during such a space, inquirieinquiry may be made, whether there be any iustjust cause, which may hinder the consummation of Marriagemarriage: considering that before the parties come and conuerseconverse together, what is amisseamiss may be remedied and amended, which to do afterward will be too late. Thirdly, In these cases, persons espoused must hauehave regard of honestiehonesty, as well as of necessitienecessity; not presently vponupon the Contractcontract, seeking to satisfiesatisfy their own fleshly desires, after the manner of bruit beasts, but proceeding therein vponupon mature deliberation.
The Contractcontract is a mention or mutuallmutual promise of future mariagemarriage, before fit and competent IudgesJudges and Witnesses.

The best manner of giuinggiving this promise, is, to make itIn verb • is de praesenti 〈…〉 . in words touching the present time, and simpliesimply without any
exception or condition expressed or conceiuedconceived. For by this meanesmeans it comes to passepass, that the bond is made the surer, and the ground or foundation of future mariagemarriage the better laid. And hence alone it is, that the persons betrothed in Scripture are termed man and wife. IacobJacob speaking of RahelRachel, who was only betrothed vntounto him, saith to Laban, GiueGive me my wife, Genes. 29. 21. Deut. 22. 23. If a maid beebe betrothed to a husband, and a man find her in the townetown, and lie with her, then shall yeeye bring them both out vntounto the gates of the citiecity, and shall stone them with stones to death, the maid, because she cried not being in the citiecity, and the man, because heehe hath humbled his neighbours wife. Matth. 1. 20. IosephJoseph fearefear not to take Mary thy wife.

Now if the promise beebe vttereduttered in words,In futurum. for time to come, it doth not precisely bind the parties to performance. For example, if one of them saith to the other; N. I will take thee, &c. andAnd not, N. I do take thee, &c. byBy this formeform of speech the match is not made, but only promised to beebe made afterward. But if
on the other side it be said, N. I do take thee, and not, I will take thee; by these termesterms, the mariagemarriage at that very instant is begun,Non de facto, de i • ure. not in regard of fact, yet in regard of right and intrestinterest, which the parties hauehave each in another in deed and in truth. And this is the common opinion of the learned. Yet notwithstanding, if the parties contracting shall say each to other, I will take thee to, &c. withWith intention to bind themseluesthemselves at the present; the bond is in conscience precisely made before God, and so the Contractcontract is indeed madeDe praesenti. for the present time before God. True it is, that he which standeth to his promise made, as much as in him lieth, doth well: yet if the promise hath or conceiuethconceiveth some iustjust cause, why heehe should afterward change his purpose, the Contractcontract expressed in termesterms for time to come, though it were formerly made, & confirmed by oath, must notwithstanding giuegive place to the Contractcontract made for time present.

Those espousals, which are made vponupon condition, which is honest, possible,
and belonging to Mariagemarriage, doedo cease or depend: so far forth as the condition annexed ceaseth or dependeth. For example; If the one partieparty promiseth to marry the other vponupon cōditioncondition, that his or her kinsman will yeeldyield consent to the match; or vponupon condition of a dowriedowry that sheeshe shall bring vntounto him, sutablesuitable to her education, and the familiefamily whereof she commeth: these conditions being kept or not kept, the promise doth likewise stand, or not stand.

But those conditions which are necessarily vnderstoodunderstood, or which may certainly be kept and come to passepass, do neither hinder nor suspend Marriagemarriage. As this: I promise thee mariagemarriage, if I liuelive; or, I promise to mariemary thee, if the SunneSun rise to morrow.

AgaineAgain, conditions that are either impossible or dishonest, are not to beebe accounted as promises annexedJn sauorem Matrimony. in way of Marriagemarriage. Of which sort are these, I will be thy wife, if thou willtwilt take vntounto thee wings and fliefly, or, If thou wilt bring an vntimelyuntimely birth.

Furthermore, if the parties betrothed, do lie together before the condition (though honest & appertaining to mariagemarriage) be performed; then the contract for time to come is, without further controuersiecontroversy, sure and certainecertain. For where there hath been a carnallcarnal vseuse of each others bodiebody, it is alwaiesalways presupposed, that a mutuallmutual consent, as touching Mariagemarriage, hath gone before.

div.head: CHAP. 5.
Of the choiseChoicechoice of personsPersons fitFit for Marriage.
div.p: FOrFor the making of a cōtractcontract, two things are requisite: first the choice, & then the consent of the parties.
Choice is an enquirieenquiry after persons mariageablemarriageable.
Persons mariageablemarriageable, are such as be fit and able for the mariedmarried state.
This fitnesfitness or abilitieability is knowneknown and discerned by certainecertain signessigns; which are either essentiallessential to the contract, or accidentallaccidental.
An essentiallessential signesign is that, without which the contract in hand becomes a meeremere nullitienullity. And of this sort there are principally fiuefive.

The first is the distinction of the sex, which is either male, or female. The male is man of a superioursuperior sexesex, fit for procreation. The female is woman of an inferiourinferior sexesex, fit to conceiueconceive and bearebear children. 1. Cor. 11. 7. The man ought not to couercover his head; for as much as he is the Imageimage and glorieglory of God; but the woman is the glorieglory of the man. 1. Tim. 2. 12. I permit not the woman to teach, neither to vsurpeusurp authoritieauthority ouerover the man, but to be in silence. By this distinction is condemned, that vnnaturalunnatural and monstrous sin of vncleannesuncleanness betweenebetween parties of the same sexesex,Rom. 1. 26 commonly termed SodomieSodomy; as also the confusion of theSpecies. kinds of creatures, when one kind commits filthinessefilthiness and abomination with another.Leuit. 18 22. 23.
The second signesign, is, the iustjust & lawfu • lllawful distance of blood.

Distance of blood is then iustjust and lawfulllawful, when neither of the persons
that are to be married, do come nearenear to the kindred of their flesh, or to the flesh of their flesh, for so the Scripture speaketh, LeuitLevit 18. 6. No man shall come nearenear to any of the flesh of his flesh: or to the Ebr. שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉
kindred of his flesh. Where it is to be obseruedobserved, that by a mans flesh is meant that substance which is of himselfehimself, or whereof himselfehimself consisteth. And by the flesh of his flesh, that which next and immediately issueth out of that flesh whereof he consisteth. Whereupon it followeth, that the touching or commingcoming nearenear of flesh to flesh, is not spoken of strangers, but of those only that are of kindred.
Kindred is of two sorts, consanguinitieconsanguinity, or affinitieaffinity.

Kindred in consanguinitieconsanguinity, are those which issue from out, & the same common blood or stockestock. And there be certainecertain degrees, whereby kinsmen of this sort are distinguished one from another.

A degree is a generation or descent betweenebetween two persons that are of the same blood. For one person cannot
make a degree, vnlesseunless he be considered relatiuelyrelatively in regard of generation.

Now many degrees continued or deriuedderived from one and the same head, do make a Lineline; And a Lineline is twofold, the Right line, or the OuerthwartOverthwart, cōmonlycommonlycommonlyconmonly termed collaterallcollateral.
In the Right Lineline, lookelook how maniemany persons there are, so many degrees there be, that only excepted, which vponupon occasion offered, is in question, and from which we begin the account.

The Right line is either ascending or descending.

The right line ascending, is the race of all the ancestors; and it hath sundriesundry degrees. Of the first whereof is, the father
and the mother; of the second, the grand-father both by the father and mothers side, that is, the father of my father, and the father of my mother; and the grand-mother, that is to say, my fathers and my mothers mother. Of the third, is, the great grand-father, or the father of my grand-father; and the great grand-mother, or the mother of my grand-father. Of the fourth, is the great grand-fathers father, and the great grand-fathers, or grand-mothers mother. Of the fiftfifth, is the great grand-fathers grand-father, & the great grand-fathers, or great grand-mothers grand-mother. Of the sixtsixth, is the great great grand-fathers grand-father; & the great great grand-fathers, or great great grand-mothers grand-mother.

The right line descending, is the race of a mans owneown posteritieposterity. And that also hath sundriesundry degrees. The first wherofwhereof is, the sonneson and the daughter; the second, the nephew, and the neeceniece; the third, the nephewesnephews sonneson, and the neecesnieces daughter. The fourth is the nephewesnephews nephew, or the sonneson in the

The fiftfifth is heehe and she that are three linealllineal descents from the childs child. And so are the rest in their order, by what names soeuersoever they be called and knowneknown.

Now in this right line, whether ascending or descending, the person, of whom the case or question is mouedmoved, commeth neerenear to the kindred of his flesh. And therefore mariagesmarriages in this line are prohibited infinitlyinfinitely, without any limitation; so as if Adam himselfehimself were now aliuealive, he could not marry by the law of God, because heehe should come nearenear to the kindred of his owneown flesh, as Moses speaketh. The reason hereof is, because in the right line, superiourssuperiors and inferioursinferiors are to each other as parents and children; and the kindred betweenebetween parents & children, being the first and nearest of all other, their coniuctionconjunction in marriage must needs beebe most vncleaneunclean, and repugnant vntounto nature.

The collaterallcollateral or crooked line, is
that, which walketh by the sides of the right line, whether ascending or descending, in the row of the kindred. And it is either vnequallunequal or equallequal.
The vnequallunequal is that, whereby the person in question and his kinsman, are vnequallyunequally distant from the common stockestock, or head of the kindred.
And in this line, lookelook how many degrees the kinsman that is furthest off from the common stock, is distant from the same, so many is he and his kinsman in question distant one from the other.

Furthermore, kinsmen in this Lineline are of two sorts; some are SuperioursSuperiors to the person in question, some are InferioursInferiors to him.
SuperioursSuperiors are such, as are a kinnekin to his father, and mother, of some side; and that either nearer, or further off.

The equallequal collaterallcollateral line, is that,
whereby kinsmen are equally distant from their head.
Kinsmen of this line, are,

II. The brothers children or cousin germans; that is, the vnclesuncles sons or daughters, or the aunts sonnessons or daughters. The sisters children, or cousin germans; that is, the aunts sonnessons or daughters, which are the children of two sisters.

In this line, lookelook how many degrees the partieparty in question is remouedremoved from the common stockestock, by so many twice-told,

div.p: HeereHere Bethuel being two degrees remouedremoved from ThareTerah, is fourefour degrees distant from Isaac.
Now he that is in the second degree of this line, comes nearenear to the kindred of his flesh; and for that cause the mariagesmarriages of brethren, and sisters are vnlawfullunlawful, and forbidden.
But against this, sundriesundry things are alledgedalleged.

ObiectObject. 1. The sons of Adam, who were the first brethren in the world, married their sisters; marriages therefore in this degree may seemeseem to beebe lawfulllawful. Answ. The case of those persons in those times, was a case of necessitienecessity, which could not be auoidedavoided, and theruponthereupon was warranted by diuinedivine dispensation. For God had giuengiven them his
owneown expresseexpress commandementcommandment in this behalfebehalf; BeareBear fruits and multipliemultiply, Gen. 1. 28. Besides that, there were then no other women in the world, by whom they might hauehave issue and posteritieposterity, but only by their sisters. Whereupon it is manifest, that Gods will was, to permit them to take eueneven their sisters to their wiueswives. But now out of this speciallspecial dispensation from God, such matching is vtterlyutterly vnlawfullunlawful, being an apparent breach of another expresseexpress commandementcommandment giuengiven afterward by God himselfehimself, LeuitLevit. 18. 9. 11. To this purpose saith Augustine in way of answereanswer to the example propounded.De ciuit. The practise of those first times, Dei. lib. 15 • . ca. 16. then backed by vrgenturgent nenessitienecessity; the more ancient it was, the more damnable it prouedproved afterward, when it was restrained by Gods commandementcommandment.

ObiectObject. 2. Sarah was Abrahams sister, and yet Abraham tooketook her to wife. Gen. 20. 12. Yet in very deed she is my sister, for she is the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother, and sheeshe is my wife. Gen. 11. 29. Abraham and Nahor tooketook them wiueswives, and the name of Abrahams
wife was Sarah. Answ. Touching this instance, there are sundriesundry opinions. The IewesJews doedo grant thus much, that she was called by a name common to all kinsfolkekinsfolk of that sexesex, to wit, a Sister; yet indeed sheeshe was Abrahams neeceniece, the sister of Lot, and the daughter of Haran, Abrahams brother, which Moses elsewhere calleth Iischa, Genes. 11. 29. Others thinkethink, that sheeshe was daughter in law to ThareTerah, Abrahams father; because Abraham himselfehimself saith, She is the daughter of my father, not of my mother. Others are of opinion, that she was Harans daughter in law, and after his death was translated into the family of Terah, her grand-father; who was also in stea • d of her father being dead, and thence sheeshe was termed his daughter Now howsoeuerhowsoever in this varietievariety of iudgementsjudgements, it is hard to find certaintiecertainty of truth, yet this is out of doubt, that God in those daiesdays tolerated many things, which notwithstanding he did not altogether approueapprove.

ObiectObject. 3. 2. Sam. 13. 13. Thamar saiessays to her brother Amnon; SpeakeSpeak I pray thee
to the King, and he will not deniedeny meeme vntounto thee. Ans. The speech of Thamar is not simpliesimply to be taken, as if she desired that which she said, or as if it were lawfulllawful to be done, which she wished him to do; but only that she sought to put him off, by giuinggiving him this counsellcounsel, in respect of her owneown deliuerancedeliverance from that present danger; wherein sheeshe was. Or at least it way be said, that she erroniouslyerroneously supposed it was lawfulllawful for the King to grant such a sutesuit, if it had binbeen made vntounto him by her brother Amnon. Whether way soeuersoever this speech beebe taken, there can no such thing beebe gathered thence, as is pretended.

Now out of the second degree of the equal collateral line, it should seemeseem that those who are ioynedjoined one to another in mariagemarriage, do not touch the kindred of their flesh; and therefore the law of God forbiddeth not cōsobrinesconsobrines or cousin-germans, that is, brothers and sisters children to marriemarry.

Yea if examples be of force for this purpose, the Scripture approuethapproves such mariagesmarriages. For thus it is written, that IacobJacob
married RahelRachel the daughter of Laban, his mothers brother, Genes. 28. 2. AgaineAgain, that Mahlah, Tirzah, and Hoglah, Milcah and Noah the daughters of Zelophehad, were married vntounto their fathers brothers sonnessons, Numb. 36. 11. And Othniel the sonneson of Kenaz, the cousin of Caleb, tooketook Kiriath-sepher; and heehe gauegave him AcsahAchsah his daughter to wife, IosJos. 15. 17.

Howbeit in this case, the rule of the Apostle is to be followed; That nothing be done, eueneven in things that are otherwise lawfulllawful, whereby a mans brother may stumble, or beebe offended, or made weakeweak, Rom. 14. 21. Wherefore it is conuenientconvenient, that such mariagesmarriages should not be, because sometimes they may giuegive offence in regard of the law of the Magistrate; and because they come somewhat nearenear to the bonds and termesterms of blood and stockestock, which God hath set downedown in his word. Augustine in his 15. bookeBook, De ciuitate Dei, chap. 16. saithSaith to this purpose, Experti autem sumus, &c. thatThat is, We hauehave found by experience, that in regard of that neerenessenearness of blood, which cousin-germans hauehave vntounto the degrees of
brothers and sisters, how rarely customecustom hath admitted those mariagesmarriages, which were warrantable by laweslaws, because the law of God hath not forbidden them, nor as yet the law of man. NeuerthelesseNevertheless the practise lawfulllawful in it selfeself, was forborne the rather, because it came nearenear to that which was vnlawfullunlawful, and therforetherefore mariagemarriage with the cousin-german, seemed in a manner to be marriage with a mans own brother or sister, &c. Howbeit, there is no question, but in these times it hath been well prouidedprovided by laweslaws, that such mariagesmarriages should not be vndertakenundertaken. For as the multiplication of alliance is hindered thereby, so this inconuenienceinconvenience also groweth from them, that friendship and louelove which is procured by affinitieaffinity, betweenebetween men that are strangers; cannot be enlarged and encreasedincreased, where men goego not out of the limits, and termesterms of their owneown blood; Yea, there is naturally in man a commendable measure of shamefastnesseshamefastness, whereby vponupon consideration of nearenessenearness in bloo • d, heehe acknowledgeth a due debt of modestiemodesty and honor to his next kindred, and consequently estrainethrestraineth himself in regard of them from he occasions and actions of concupiscence,
whereunto heehe is inclinable in respect of others. And hence it is, that generally the modestiemodesty that ought to be in those which intend mariagemarriage, auoidethavoideth as much as may be, these and such like coniunctionsconjunctions. Cor. 6. but all things are not expedient.

But it is auouchedavouched to the contrariecontrary, that God by expresseexpress law forbiddeth mariagemarriage with the aunt, the fathers sister LeuitLevit. 18. 12. andAnd with the mothers sister▪, vers. 13. andAnd with the fathers brother wife, which is also the aunt, vers. 14. thereforeTherefore by the law of proportion, it •
forbiddeth matching with the children ••
of these persons. For in nature it is a ruled case: If a man may not marriemarry the •
mother, much lesseless may he marriemarry the daughter.

Answ. The argument is faultiefaulty, and concludes nothing to the purpose. For there is not the same reason of both. In the right line of consanguinitieconsanguinity, those which are sisters to father and mother, stand in the place and stead of parents; and their nephewesnephews and neecesnieces are to them as children, therefore mariagesmarriages among them can stand by no law, either of God, of nature, or by the positiuepositive laweslaws of nations. It is not so with cousin germans. For hauinghaving no such relation, there is not in their mariagesmarriages, by the law of Moses, any discoueriediscovery of shame, or breach of ciuilcivil honestiehonesty. The blessing of God vponupon some of them mentioned in Scripture, as vponupon IacobJacob and RahelRachel, and such like, doedo euidentlyevidently shewshow that they were lawfulllawful in themseluesthemselves, and pleasing vntounto him. And thus much touching kindred by blood or consanguinitieconsanguinity.

Kindred in affinitieaffinity, is that, whereby the termesterms of two kindreds, are brought into the societiesociety of one and the same
familiefamily; or whereby persons that are not of blood, are by marriage allied each to other. Hence it is termed affinitieaffinity, because it maketh an vnitieunity of termesterms in kindred, which before were distant.

Affinity or alliance groweth by mixtion or participation of blood, in the coupling of man and wife together in lawfulllawful mariagemarriage. For a bare and simple contract, maketh not alliance betweenebetween partieparty and partieparty properly, but mariagemarriage after the contract finished and consummate.

AgaineAgain, the same alliance ceaseth and determineth vponupon the death of either partieparty espoused or mariedmarried; yet so as the prohibition of coniunctionconjunction remainesremains, and stands in force, for the preseruationpreservation of publikepublic honestiehonesty.

Now there is a kind of resemblance and proportion betweenebetween kindred of blood, and kindred by mariagemarriage, not only in regard of degrees and line, but also in respect of the prohibition of degrees.

Those that are of alliance, are commonly
reduced to these heads.

II. Rulerule. Cousins by mariagemarriage within the degrees, both of the right and collaterallcollateral line, doedo come neerenear to the kindred of their flesh, in the same manner that cousins by bloudblood doedo, in the same lines; and the like degrees in both are forbidden. Therefore in the right line of affinitieaffinity, it is as well vnlawfulunlawful for the father in law to marriemarry the daughter in law, or the sonneson in law to marry the mother in law; as it is for the father to marriemarry the daughter, or the sonneson the mother. AgaineAgain, in the collaterallcollateral, it is as vnlawfulunlawful for the vncleuncle by the mothers side, to marriemarry the wife of his sisters son, and so in other degrees, as it is for him to match in the same degrees of cōsanguinitieconsanguinitieconsanguinity. The reason is, because in these lines, as well as in those of consanguinitieconsanguinity,
superiourssuperiors and inferioursinferiors, are each to other as parents and children.

From hence amongst other things, it may beebe gathered, that it is in no sort lawful for a man, when his wife is dead, to marriemarry her sister, LeuitLevit. 18. 16. Thou shalt not discouerdiscover the shame of thy brothers wife; for it is thy brothers shame. And LeuitLevit. 20. 21. The man that taketh his brothers wife, committethcommiteth filthinesfilthiness, because he hath vncouereduncovered his brothers shame.

Against this doctrine it is obiectedobjected. First, that God commandeth not to take a wife with her sister, during her life, LeuitLevit. 18. 18. inIn which place, heehe doth not simpliesimply forbid a man to marry two sisters one after another, but to marriemarry them both together, and therefore after the wife is dead, a man may marriemarry her sister.

Ans. The place is a flat prohibition of the sin of PolygamiePolygamy. For to take a wife to her sister in the Hebrew phrase, is nothing else but to take two wiueswives one to another. The like formeform of speech is vsedused otherwhere by Moses, as Exo. 26. 3.

FiueFive curtainescurtains shall beebe coupled together, [the woman to her sister] that is, one to another; and the other fiuefive curtainescurtains shall be coupled [the woman to her sister] that is, the one to the other. Ezech. 1. 9. The fourefour beasts were ioynedjoined with their wings, [the woman to her sister] that is, the one to the other. AgaineAgain, Moses himselfehimself there alledgethallegeth two reasons against PolygamiePolygamy: the one is, because the man is to louelove, cherish and comfort this wife; whereas, if he should take vntounto him another besides her, he should greatly vex his first lawfulllawful wife. The other, because by that meanesmeans he should vncoueruncover the shame of his wife; that is, he should play a very dishonest part with her, to whom he was before lawfully married.
ObiectObject. 2 The Lord commanded by a speciallspecial law, that the brother, in case his brother died without issue, should take his wife, and raise vpup seedeseed vntounto him, Deut. 25. 5.

Answ. The words of Moses are a speciallspecial exception of a generallgeneral law propounded in LeuitLevit. 18. 16. Thou shalt not discouerdiscover the shame of thy brothers wife; for
it is thy brothers shame. And they are peculiarly directed to the Israelites, vponupon speciallspecial cause; that, when the elder brother died without seed the name of the first borne might not be extinct, but the familiefamily might beebe preseruedpreserved in that name, by raising vpup of seed vntounto him, which being a priuiledgeprivilege proper to the Israelites, vponupon that speciallspecial consideration, it must not beebe enlarged to any other sort of men whatsoeuerwhatsoever. Neither is the text to be vnderstoodunderstood of cousins remouedremoved only, as some thinkethink, but also of the next of the kindred by blood; as appeareth plainly by the historiehistory of Ruth, chap. I. versVers. II. inIn these words of Naomi to her daughters in law, TurneTurn againeagain, my daughters; for what cause will you go with me? Are there any moe sonnessons in my wombewomb, that they may beebe your husbands? TurneTurn againeagain, my daughters, go your way, for I am too old to hauehave a husband, &c.

III. Rulerule. The wiueswives kinsman by blood, is of affinitieaffinity to her husband only; but vntounto his kindred by blood, the said kinsman hath no affinitieaffinity at all. So
on the contrariecontrary it is true, that though the husbands kinsman by blood, be allied to his wife, yet he hath no alliance to those that are kinsmen of blood vntounto her. The reason is, because betweenebetween the kindred of blood on the mans side, and the kindred of blood on the womans side, there is no affinitieaffinity. For the prohibition of the degrees of affinitieaffinity, hath force in those only which are the cause thereof, and goeth no further. Now the cause being only in the married persons themseluesthemselves, the effect may not in reason be enlarged, to them that are of the same blood with either of them.

From this rule it followeth, that the kindred of both married persons by blood, may lawfully match together. The sonneson in law, may match with the daughter of his mother in law. The father and the son by another wife, may marriemarry the mother and the daughter. Two brothers may lawfully match with two sisters.

IV. Rulerule. Kindred of affinitieaffinity to the wife,Beza de repudijs. 82. are also kindred of affinitieaffinity to her
husband; but how? notNot properly, but only after a sort, and as it were, of affinitieaffinity. So on the contrariecontrary. Kindred of alliance to the husband, are, as it were, of alliance to his wife. For example. The wife of my father in law, which is not my wiueswives owneown mother, but her step-mother, is, as it were, my mother in law, for she is (as it were) of affinitieaffinity to me, because she is indeed of affinitieaffinity to my wife.

Those which are of affinitieaffinity only after a sort, cannot conuenientlyconveniently match one with another. And therefore the sonneson in law may not marriemarry with his wiueswives step-mother; because being of affinitieaffinity to his wife, sheeshe is in stead of a mother in law to him. Neither may the daughter in law match with her husbands step-father, because heehe is (as it were) a step-father to her. AgaineAgain, my sisters husband may not marry my brothers wife; for they are after a sort, brother and sister each to other. The reason hereof is, because the wife is holden in law aCuius nuptias ini • re non licet, eius nec coniug • is licet. part of her husband, and therforetherefore if affinitieaffinity hinders mariagemarriage with
one of the married couples, it hindreth as well in the like case and respect, mariagemarriage with the other.

And thus much touching the distance of blood, which in the choice of persons fit for mariagemarriage, is most necessarily to be obseruedobserved. For in the 18. chapterChapter of LeuiticusLeviticus, there are sixteenesixteen seuerallseveral sorts of persons with whom mariagemarriage is forbidden. The first is the mother. The second is the step-mother. The thidthird, the sister by the same father and mother. The fourth, the half-sister, by one of the parents only. The fifth is the neeceniece by the sonneson. The sixth, the neeceniece by the daughter. The seuenthseventh, the fathers sister. The eight, the vnclesuncles, that is, the fathers brothers wife. The ninth, the mothers sister. The tenth, the daughter in law, or sons wife. The eleuentheleventh, the brothers wife. The twelfth, the wiueswives mother. The thirteenth, the step-daughter, or the wiueswives daughter by another husbādhusband, or husbādshusbands daughter by a former wife. another husbādhusband. The fifteenth, the step-daughters daughter. The sixteenth, is the wiueswives sister. And not only these, but all other answerable to them, either in the same or like degree, are by equallequal proportion forbidden to be had in mariagemarriage.
It is alledgedalleged, that the prohibitions mentioned in that chapter, are meerelymerely MosaicallMosaic, that is, CeremoniallCeremonial, and therefore doedo not bind vsus now in the new Testament.
Answ. It is a flat vntruthuntruth; as shall appeareappear by these reasons.

First, the Cananites long before these laweslaws were giuengiven by Moses to the Israelites, were grieuouslygrievously afflicted for the breach and contempt of the same, as may beebe gathered by that which is written in the same chapter of LeuiticusLeviticus, Chap. 18. vers. 3. Secondly, the Prophets themseluesthemselves after Moses, are wont to account these prohibitions not Ceremonial, but MorallMoral. Ezech. 22. 10. In thee, hauehave they discouereddiscovered their fathers shame; in thee hauehave they vexed her, that was polluted in her flowers. Amos 2. 7. Thirdly, the same laweslaws are also vrgedurged in the new Testament, wherinwherein Legal Ceremonies were determined, and had their end. Mark. 6. 18. Fourthly, Naturenature it selfeself by proper instinct, abhorreth such kind of coniunctionsconjunctions, & the prohibitions of them, hauehave sufficient ground, eueneven from her principles. For to this purpose it is, that not only the laweslaws of the RomaneRoman EmperoursEmperors,

FiftlyFifthly, The Lord himselfehimself hath denounced many and great punishments to be inflicted vponupon the breach of the same laweslaws. LeuitLevit. 20. 11. Deut. 23. 2. A bastard shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord, eueneven to his tenth generation. Deut. 27. 20. Cursed be he that lieth with his fathers wife.

The third essential Signesign of a person mariageablemarriageable, is abilitieability and fitnessefitness for procreation. And this in an holy and modest sort is alwaiesalways supposed to beebe in the partieparty contracted, vnlesseunless the cōtrariecontrariecontrary be manifestly knowneknown, & discerned by some apparent infirmitieinfirmity in the bodiebody.

Hence I gather, that it is vnlawfulunlawful to make a contract with such a person, as is vnfitunfit for the vseuse of mariagemarriage, either by naturallnatural constitution of bodiebody, or by accident. For example; in regard of sicknessesickness, or of frigiditiefrigidity, or of the palsiepalsy vncurableuncurable, or lastly of the depriuationdeprivation of the parts belonging to generation. These and such like impediments are of force, though a contract should alreadiealready be made, yet to make it a meeremere nullitienullity, considering that God maketh knowneknown his will in them, that heehe approouethapproves not of such espousals, but would hauehave them to be dissolueddissolved.

AgaineAgain, that which is made betweenebetween two persons that areImpuberes. vnderunder age, is to beebe holden and accounted as vnlawfullunlawful. And though it should be done by consent, or cōmandementcommandementcommandment of Parentsparents, yet it is of no moment. This alwaiesalways remembredremembered; except it beebe ratified by a new consent of the parties after they be come to age; or that they in the meanemean time hauehave had priuateprivate and carnallcarnal copulation one with another.

AgaineAgain, put the case two be espoused, whereof the one is vnderunder age, the other of full age; the partieparty that is of full age, ought to tarrietarry and expect the time, wherein the issue of the espousals formerly made, may beebe manifested. Whereupon it followeth, that a promise of mariagemarriage made betweenebetween those, whereof the one hath a disease so lothsomeloathsome, as that the other vponupon good ground cannot possibliepossibly endure familiar societiesociety and companiecompany with him; though it do not wholly hinder the vseuse of the bodiebody, is vtterlyutterly vnlawfullunlawful.

Of this sort is the LeprosieLeprosy, the FrēchFrench poxepox and such like. For seeing there cannot be any matrimonial vseuse of them that are tainted with such contagious diseases, without apparent danger of infecting each other, and those also, which hauehave societiesociety with them, and others; yea and by this meanesmeans the issue of their bodies, growing of a corrupted seed, are eueneven borne to perpetual miseriemisery, and to the great hurt and hinderancehindrance of the Commoncommon-wealth; the case is plaineplain, that such mariagesmarriages cannot be vndertakenundertaken with good conscience.

Now if the one party hauehave a disease, though not contagious, yet either incurable, or soTurpi. lothsomeloathsome, as the other hath iustjust cause to abhor his companiecompany; for example, if he be sickesick of a LethargieLethargy,
of the falling sicknessickness, or such like diseases; then, though it be lawfulllawful to match with him, because such a contract is not expresselyexpressly forbidden, neither is it apparantlyapparently hurtfullhurtful to the CōmonCommoncommon-wealth, yet is it not expedient, because the disease being lothsomeloathsome to the sound partieparty, the mariagemarriage also will become vnprofitableunprofitable, and the partieparty in danger of breaking the commandemētcommandementcommandment of the MorallMoral law, wherein God forbiddeth to commit adulterieadultery.

The fifth essentiallessential Signesign of a person mariageablemarriageable, is freedomefreedom from mariagemarriage; whereby both the parties which enter contract, are so at libertieliberty, that neither the man hath in present another wife, or is promised to another; nor the woman hath another husband, or is promised to another. The reason is, because God himselfehimself esteemeth that mariagemarriage only lawfulllawful, wherein one man is ioynedjoined to one woman, and they both into one flesh; & consequently iudgethjudgeth it vnlawfullunlawful, as for one man to hauehave more wiueswives; so for one woman at the same time to hauehave more husbands.

Hence it followeth, that it is against the law of God, and the first institution of mariagemarriage, that a contract should beebe made betweenebetween such persons, whereof the one is formerly betrothed to another. For so long as the first promise stands in force, the man can no more be betrothed to two women, then he may be the husband of two wiueswives; because the spouse by the bond of her promise to the man, becomes a wife; and the man by the bond of his promise to the woman, becomes an husband, Deut. 22. 23. 24.

AgaineAgain, there can beebe no sure-making, and consequently no mariagemarriage with such a one, as either hath been diuorceddivorced without a sufficient cause, or hath wrongfully forsaken and reiectedrejected a lawfulllawful mate before. To this purpose saith our SauiourSaviour Christ, Matth. 19. 9. I say vntounto you, that whosoeuerwhosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for whoredomewhoredom, & marieth another, committethcommiteth adulterieadultery; and whosoeuerwhosoever marrieth her which is diuorceddivorced, committethcommiteth adulterieadultery. And Saint Paul, 1. Cor. 7. 11. But & if she depart, let her remaineremain
vnmarriedunmarried, or be reconciled vntounto her husband, and let not the husband put away his wife.
Hitherto I hauehave treated of essentiallessential markesmarks, which belong to the being of mariagemarriage. Now I come to those that are accidentallaccidental.

An accidentallaccidental markemark of a person fit for mariagemarriage, is that, which belongeth not to the being, but to the well being, that is, to the holinesholiness and puritiepurity of that estate. And of this sort, there be three that are the principallprincipal.

The first is paritieparity or equality, in regard of Christian religion; For in mariagemarriage, there is a speciallspecial care to be had, that belieuersbelievers be matched with belieuersbelievers, and Christians with Christians; not belieuersbelievers with Infidels, or Christians with Pagans. For the former sort are only and alwaiesalways to be made and kept, and the latter to be auoidedavoided, yea inhibited by positiuepositive laweslaws and constitutions, the breach whereof in such cases is seuerelyseverely to be punished. The neglect of this point was one principallprincipal cause of the destructiōdestruction of the old world
by the floudflood. Gen. 6. 2. The sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were fairefair, and they tooketook them wiueswives of all that they liked. Abraham obseruedobserved it in the mariagemarriage of Isaac his sonneson, and for that purpose tooketook an oath of his seruantservant. Gen. 24. 3. I will make thee sweareswear by the Lord God of heauenheaven, and God of the earth, that thou shalt not take a wife vntounto my son, of the daughters of the Cananites among whom I dwell. And in imitation of that holy example, Isaac also giuesgives a charge vntounto IacobJacob his son, that he should not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan, Gen. 28. 1. Afterward there was an expresseexpress law of God giuengiven by Moses, touching the Gentiles that liuedlived in that land. Exod. 34. 15. Beware that thou make not a couenantcovenant with the inhabitants of the land, &c. versVers. 16. And take of their daughters vntounto thy sonnessons, and their daughters go a whoring after their gods; and make thy sonnessons goego a whoring after their gods. And the same law was vrgedurged by Ezra the Priest in his time. Ezra 10. 11. Separate your seluesselves from the people of the land, and from the strange wiueswives. Lastly, S. Paul
exhorteth the CorinthiāsCorinthians, 2. Cor. 6. 14. Be not vnequallyunequally yoked with the Infidels. And Titus 3. 10. ReiectReject him that is an heretikeheretic, after once or twice admonition.

But suppose it falleth out, that the espousals be past, and that both parties at the first were belieuersbelievers, or one of thēthem only; or that at first both were vnbelieuersunbelievers, and yet afterward one of them is conuertedconverted to the faith; or further, admit that both were belieuersbelievers at the contract, yet within some time after, the one becomes an InfidellInfidel, that is to say, a IewJew, a TurkeTurk, or an obstinate HeretikeHeretic, that denies the faith, and razeth eueneven the very foundation of Religion; in this case what is to be done? Surely euēeueneven such espousals once made and ended, if there be no other impediments but these, are to stand & continue firmefirm and vnchangeableunchangeable; so long as the vnbelieuingunbelieving partieparty doth willingly yeeldyield, and submit him or her selfeself to the performance of mariagemarriage duties, properly belonging to man and wife. My reason is, the speech of Paul, who saith; If any brother hauehave a wife, that beleeuethbelieveth not, if
