she be content to dwell with him, let him not forsake her. AgaineAgain, The woman which hath an husband that belieuethbelieveth not, if he be content to dwell with her, let her not forsake him, 1. Cor. 7. 12. 13.

If it be heerehere alledgedalleged, that the sin of adulterieadultery dissoluesdissolves the bond both of contract and mariagemarriage, and therefore much more doth idolatrieidolatry or infidelity, which is a sinnesin farrefar more detestable then adulterieadultery: I answereanswer, that the questiōquestion is not, whether of these is the greater sin, or more hainousheinous in the sight of God; for InfidelitieInfidelity in both respects far exceedeth the other; but whether of them is more repugnant to the nature and condition of wedlockewedlock. Now the sinnesin of adulterieadultery is that alone, which breakesbreaks the bond, and renounceth the troth plighted in mariagemarriage, and is the proper cause of a diuorcedivorce, and not IdolatrieIdolatry or InfidelitieInfidelity.
The second note, is parity or equalitieequality in regard of age and condition.

First of Age; because though the mariagemarriage of persons, whose yearesyears are farrefar vnequallunequal, is not expreslyexpressly forbidden in
the word; yet is it agreeable to the rules of expediencieexpediency and decenciedecency, that the aged should match with the aged, the yongeryounger with the yongeryounger.

Reasons are these. First, because the comforts of this societiesociety in likelihood will by this meanesmeans alwaiesalways be equallequal, and consequently bring the more contentment to either partieparty. Secondly, these vnequallunequal mariagesmarriages are often times offensiueoffensive to others. Thirdly, they cannot but in some cases proueprove offensiueoffensive eueneven to themseluesthemselves. For when a man of great yearesyears matcheth with a woman very yongyoung, or a yongyoung stripling marrieth an aged woman; the elder partieparty growing weakeweak and impotent, may the sooner come to be vnfitunfit for mariagemarriage duties; and the yongeryounger being of greater strēgthstrength and abilitieability,, the more in danger of being exposed to incontinencieincontinency, and that in the highest degree, vnlesseunless he be restrained by Gods speciallspecial grace. For this cause it was a great fault, wherewith one Apuleius was iustlyjustly charged, that being but a very yongyoung man, he was married to a wife of 60. yearesYears of age.

Secondly, of condition and estate. For this also is answerable vntounto the Apostles rule, who exhorteth men to thinkethink of, and to do those things which are true, iustjust, commendable, and of good report, Philip. 4. 8. Thus it is a seemelyseemly and commendable practise, that, the Prince, the Noble man, the free-man, the gentleman, the yeoman, &c. shouldShould be ioynedjoined in societiesociety with them, that are of the same or like condition with themseluesthemselves, and not otherwise. For this cause are the auncientancient Romans greatly to be commended, who (as we readeread in their stories) had such a carefullcareful respect of their mariagesmarriages in this behalfebehalf, that they made laweslaws and constitutions for the restraining of inequalitieinequality of worldly estate in such societies, by this meanesmeans preuentingpreventing much confusion and disturbance in families, and other orders of men. Whereunto agrees that of Tertullian, Tertul. ad vxor. li. 2. who saith, That if a free woman had affianced her selfeself to him that was a bond-man to another, and being thrice admonished thereof, by him that had authoritieauthority ouerover her, did notwithstanding perseuerepersevere
in her purpose; she should, according to the law, lose her freedomefreedom.

The third note is publikepublic honestiehonesty and credit, whereby the contract made becomes a matter of good report, well thought and spoken of abroad. WhatsoeuerWhatsoever things are of good report, thinkethink on them. Philip. 4. 8. From hence I gather,

I. That it is an vnseemelyunseemly thing for a māman to make promise of mariagemarriage to such a woman, as hath binbeen formerly deflowreddeflowered, or hath and is, or may beconuincedbe convinced of adulterieadultery & vncleannesuncleanness. Nay I addeadd further, that a cōtractcontract made with such a one, as himself hath before deflowreddeflowered, is by the law of God vnlawfullunlawful. For the adulterer and the adulteresseadulteress, by diuinedivine law should be put to death, and be cut off from humane societiesociety, LeuitLevit. 20. 10.

II. It is altogether inexpedient, that a woman should be married to such a man, as hath a Concubineconcubine, vnlesseunless heehe formerly renounce her, and testifietestify the same by true and vnfeinedunfeigned repentance. The reason is plaineplain. Such a mariagemarriage cannot be vndertakenundertaken in the Lord. And the partieparty himselfehimself, being before polluted
with his Concubineconcubine, becomes now by mariagemarriage to another, an adulterer; and she that is mariedmarried vntounto him, by this her act yeeldsyields consent vntounto his adulterieadultery.

III. That no man professing Christian religion, much lesseless a Minister of the word, ought to take to himselfehimself in mariagemarriage a harlot, a defamed woman, or one that comes of infamous parents, though she be repentant. LeuitLevit. 21. 7. The Priest shall not take to wife one that is a whore, or prophanedprofaned, that is to say, which hath an euillevil name, or comes of ignominious parents. Which law, though it was in part Ceremonial and LeuiticalLevitical, and so far forth abrogate; yet hauinghaving in it some MoralitieMorality, in as much as the reason therofthereof (to wit, because it is reprochfullreproachful to a Christian, but specially to a Minister) is still in force, it is to be holden perpetuallperpetual. For Christian profession, and the EcclesiasticallEcclesiastical MinistrieMinistry is principally to be respected, and whatsoeuerwhatsoever may preiudiceprejudice the dignitiedignity and credit thereof, to be auoidedavoided.

ObiectObject. 1. The Prophet Hosea was
commanded to take vntounto him a wife of fornication, that is, an harlot, Hosea 1. 2. Answ. Hosea did it not in deed, but in type and resemblance. For God commanded him in his prophecieprophecy, to take vponupon him (as it were) the person of a fornicator, that by this meanesmeans heehe might the more effectually charge and cōuinceconuinceconvince the Israelites of their vncleaneunclean and vnchastunchaste conuersationconversation.

ObiectObject. 2. The Lord also forbiddeth the Priest to marriemarry a widow, LeuitLevit. 21. 14. itIt may seemeseem therefore vnexpedientunexpedient for a Minister so to do. Answ. The law concerning the mariagemarriage of a virgin, and not a widow, was not enioynedenjoined to all Priests, but only to the chiefechief Priest, LeuitLevit. 21. 10. And heehe also might marriemarry a widow, but such a one only, as had binbeen the widow of a Priest, and not any other, Ezech. 44. 22. Now this was commanded them vponupon speciallspecial consideration. For the High Priest was a type of Christ, and Christ was in time to come to call his Church, the elect, among the Gentiles, and to marriemarry them as a virgin espoused vntounto himselfehimself. Yea he was also
to marriemarry his Church as a widow, but the widow of a Priest only, because he was to gather to himselfehimself the remnant of the Church of the IewesJews; howbeit not all of them, but such only as came of the holy Fathers, and were Israelites, not according to the flesh, but according to the promise.
IV. That it is not meetemeet for a man to be contracted to the sister of her that is alreadiealready affianced vntounto him.
And so much of the first point, required to the making of a contract, namely, the choice of a person fit for mariagemarriage.

div.head: CHAP. 6.
Of consentConsent in the Contract.
div.p:
THeThe second thing required to the making of a contract, is the free and full consent of the parties, which is indeed the very soulesoul and life of the contract. And this consent standeth in the approbation, or (as weewe
commonly call it) the Sure-making of the parties contracted.
Consent in this case is twofold, either of the man and the woman, or of their parents.

Touching the first; That the man and the woman may yeeldyield free consent each to other, it is necessarienecessary that, in respect of vnderstandingunderstanding, their iudgemētiudgementjudgement should be sound; and in regard of will, their choice should be free. And here sundriesundry cases are to be resoluedresolved.
I. Case. When the contract flowesflows not from the wilwill and good liking of the parties, but is forced and compelled, what is then to be done?

Ans. If the espousals hauehave binbeen made through force, or fearefear; I meanemean, such as may befall a constant, and resolute man, and which hath binbeen wrought, vponupon good knowledge, and cōsiderationconsideration; then are they of no moment, & in truth meeremere nullities; because there is wanting to them the free and voluntarievoluntary accord, and assent of both parties. NeuerthelesseNevertheless, if afterward they shall grow to a new consent, or both yeeldyield to an after-acceptation
of that which was formerly made, the espousals shall then stand in force; without further exception, or contradiction.
II. Case. But how if consent beebe past, and in processeprocess of time it appearesappears to the espoused persons, that they hauehave erred, either in choice, or consent, or both?
Answ. There is a three-fold error in consent; the one of the person, the other of the abilitieability, or estate of the person; the third of the qualitiequality.

Error in respect of the person, is, whēwhen one person is taken for another; or whēwhen the contract is made betweenebetween two, whereof the one was taken to be such a partieparty, as afterwards he prouedproved not to be. Now where this error is committed, it is a plaineplain case, there was no consent; and therefore the contract, vponupon certainecertain knowledge therofthereof, is quite frustrate. For the knowledge of the partieparty is the ground of consent, and belongs consequently to the very substance of mariagemarriage.

NeuerthelesseNevertheless, if, the error being
once knowneknown, the parties hauehave had secret societiesociety one with another; & hauehave either againeagain consented, or growengrown to an after-acceptation of the consent before made, the contract may and doth stand in full force. For example: IacobJacob, by the deceit of Laban, had taken Leah for Rachel, to his wife; so saith the text, When the eueningevening was come, Laban tooketook Leah his daughter, and brought her to him, and he went in vntounto her, Gen. 29▪. 23. But when the morning was come, behold it was Leah, 25. Now by the iudgementjudgement of the best DiuinesDivines, IacobJacob might iustlyjustly hauehave renounced Leah, if he would, because Laban had giuengiven her vntounto him for Rachel, and so deceiueddeceived him; yet heehe would not vseuse extremitieextremity, but kept her as his wife.

If it be said, there was an error in the person, therefore no consent, and so Leah was not his lawfulllawful wife, but Rachel. I answereanswer, that IacobJacob did renuerenew his cōsentconsent afterward, & that renuedrenewed cōsentconsent following vponupon their knowing one of another, made her his wife, though in extremity & rigor she was not. AgaineAgain,
Rachel was indeed the partieparty to whom he was espoused, by the former cōtractcontract; and therforetherefore, vponupon their mutuallmutual agreement afterward, she also became his wife. So saith the holy Ghost, vers. 27. Fulfill seuenseven yearesyears for her, and we will also giuegive thee Rachel for thy seruiceservice, &c. vV. 28. Then IacobJacob did so, and Laban gauegave him Rachel his daughter to be his wife.

Error of the ability or estate is, when one of the parties to whom cōsentconsent was giuengiven by the other, being taken for rich and wealthiewealthy, in the issue prouesproves to hauehave been very poorepoor, and not sufficient to maintainemaintain that state of life.

Touching this error, it is to be considered, whether the cōtractcontract was made absolute, for the time present, & so for euerever afterward, or conditional for time to come only. If it were absolute, that is, conceiuedconceived in termesterms of the present time, then though the deceit beebe verievery offensiueoffensive to the partieparty deluded, and vponupon his complaint ought in equitieequity to be punished by the Magistrate; yet it is not of force to breakebreak off the contract; because the abilitieability of either or both
parties belongs not to the essence of mariagemarriage. But if it were for time to come and conditionate, then he or she that made promise vponupon this condition, is free and not bound in conscience to fulfill the promise; vnlesseunless the condition expressed aforehand be kept, and performed.

Error of the qualitiequality of the person, is, when she which was in the espousals taken to beebe a virgin, is afterward found to be with child by another, before they come together. By this error the CouenantCovenant is made void, and becomes a meeremere nullitienullity; so as the man cannot be compelled, vponupon true and certainecertain knowledge thereof, to marriemarry the woman; but may renounce her, vnlesseunless both parties come to a new agreement, or hauehave priuatelyprivately knowneknown each other vponupon mutuallmutual consent. For first, God did in expresseexpress tearmesterms command the IewesJews, that such a woman should be stoned to death: Deut. 22. 20. If the maid (that was giuengiven to wife) be not found a virgin, vers. 21. then shall they bring the maid to the dooredoor of her fathers house, and
the men of her citiecity shalshall stone her with stones to death, because she hath wrought folly in Israel, by playing the whore in her fathers house. Therefore it was not the will of God, that she should be retained as a wife, but vtterlyutterly reiectedrejected and forsaken. AgaineAgain, this was so vsualusual a practise in Israel vponupon Gods commandementcommandment, that godly and righteous men, vponupon the discoueriediscovery of this error, would not in conscience be perswadedpersuaded, to marry thēthem to whom they had been betrothed, Matth. 1. 18. IosephJoseph her husband (hauinghaving found, before MarieMary and he came together, that she was with child) being a iustjust man, and not willing to make her a publikepublic example, was minded to put her away secretly.
III. Case. What shall we thinkethink of the espousals of such, as are furious, and frantickefrantic?
Answ. We must distinguish of these diseases. For MadnesMadness is, either perpetuallperpetual, or by fits only with intermission.

If it be perpetuallperpetual, the case is cleereclear, that whether one of the parties only, or both be frantickefrantic, the contract made
betweenebetween them, is altogether vnprofitableunprofitable & vainevain. For such know not what they do whēwhen they make a promise, and the consent which passeth betwixt thēthem cannot be free, full and perfect, but must needs be hindredhindered and preiudicedprejudiced by the heateheat and violence of their disease.

Now although perpetuallperpetual madnessemadness be a iustjust impediment of mariagemarriage, and a sufficient cause to dissoluedissolve a contract, yet it is meet that there be a conuenientconvenient space of time agreed vponupon, wherein all meanesmeans may be vsedused for the curing of this disease, to the end that Gods wilwill touching their amendment may be the more euidentlyevidently knowneknown; and both the parties themseluesthemselves, and their friends may giuegive testimonietestimony to the world, that they hauehave had a carefullcareful respect of the contract before made.

AgaineAgain, if it be not continuallcontinual, but by Dilucida interualla. fits, so as they hauehave some good daiesdays, and quiet intermissiōintermission, the case is otherwise. For the contract shall be ratified, and stand in force: prouidedprovided, that it was manifestly knowneknown, that the said parties
were both in their right wits, before they plight their troth each to other; and themseluesthemselves be willing afterwards to confirmeconfirm their promise former • ly made, by renuingrenewing their consent.
Consent of the Parentsparents, is that act whereby they giuegive their word and promise, to bestow their children in mariagemarriage, and in regard of right, doedo indeed presently bestow them.

Therefore priuateprivate contracts, that are made without free and lawfulllawful consent of parents, are not only vnprofitableunprofitable and vnlawfullunlawful, but eueneven by the law of God meeremere nullities. Reasons. I. They are contrariecontrary to the expresseexpress will and commandementcommandment of God: Exod. 20. Honorhonor thy father and thy mother. II. They are flat repugnant to naturallnatural equitieequity; which teacheth, that he who hath not power, nor right ouerover himselfehimself, cannot bind himselfehimself by promise to another. Now children hauehave not power ouerover themseluesthemselves,Gal. 4. 1. but are vnderunder the gouernmentgovernment, & at the disposition of their Parentsparents; therefore the couenantscovenants which they make, are not made and appointed
of God, and those which God maketh not, are in deed and truth none at all.

div.head: CHAP. 7.
Of ReiectionRejection, or RefusallRefusal of the Contract.
div.p: COntraryContrary to a complete and lawful cōtractcontract,Repudium. is ReiectionRejection, wherbywhereby the Contractcontract is dissolueddissolved, or broken off.

A lawfulllawful Contractcontract is then dissolueddissolved, when some great and hainousheinous fault followeth immediately vpōvponupon it, in either of the parties espoused. And from hēcehence arise diuersdivers and sundriesundry cases to be set downedown and resoluedresolved.
The first is this. What is to be done, when some disease befalsbefalls one of the parties immediately after the contract made?

Answ. Those diseases which take away the vseuse of the bodiebody, and altogether disable the partieparty from the performance of the promise made, in respect of mariagemarriage
duties, are very iustjust impediments of mariagemarriage, and consequently do break off the Contractcontract. Of which sort are vncurableuncurable palsies, frigiditiefrigidity, and such like, whereof I hauehave spoken before.

NeuerthelesseNevertheless a couenātcouenantcovenant once made, is not suddenly to beebe renounced, for fearefear of breeding offence. And therefore some longer respite is to be taken from the time of the contract, in which they are to rest in expectation of amēdmentamendment, before the said diseases be publikelypublicly and solemnelysolemnly declared to be incurable, and consequently that the couenantcovenant made is become void.

Now, if the disease do not for the present take away the vseuse of the body, and yet in time prouesproves incurablieincurably contagious, and so lothsomeloathsome, that the one may iustlyjustly fearefear to keepekeep and conuerseconverse with the other; as it falleth out when one is tainted with leprosieleprosy; then the contract is vtterlyutterly to be dissolueddissolved, as if God himself should hauehave commanded it, though the promise was formerlieformerly made, & the parties themseluesthemselves should be vnwillingunwilling. God hath ordained MatrimonieMatrimony
to helpehelp, not to hurt either the persons themseluesthemselves, or others. Where therefore these diseases be, which may infect, hurt, or destroy others, there God hath, as it were, testified from heauenheaven, that the act done is not pleasing vntounto him, and that presently it ought to be frustrate.

The contract being thus once dissolueddissolved, the sounder partieparty shall be at his, or her libertieliberty to marriemarry againeagain. But the diseased is by the Magistrates authoritieauthority, to be forbidden societiesociety with any other in way of mariagemarriage, and commanded to lead his life, where he may conuenientlyconveniently from companiecompany, for fearefear of infection. And withal he is for his owneown part, to sue vntounto God by prayer in faith for the gift of continenciecontinency. For certainecertain it is, that he to whom God hath denied the power of vsingusing mariagemarriage with good conscience, is thereby eueneven called to continenciecontinency and single life.

But if the disease be not contagious, yet either incurable, or so nastienasty, that either of the espoused hath iustjust cause to be afraid of the others companiecompany; then
both are to be aduisedadvised, not to claimeclaim their right, but willingly to surrender it each to other by mutuallmutual consent, that they may be free againeagain, & not bound by any former promise to liuelive together as man and wife. Considering that they hauehave no hope mutually to conuerseconverse together, with comfort & contentment, while they so remaineremain.

VponUpon this aduiceadvice giuengiven by their lawfulllawful Pastor, or some in his stead; if they both yeeldyield, or one of them at the least desires to be at his owneown libertieliberty, the espousals are forthwith to be brokēbroken off. But if neither will consent to a separation, but rather proceed as they hauehave begun, and in probability the one hauehave no iustjust cause to hold the other in suspitionsuspicion, in respect of contagion; they are not to be hindered from the consummation of their mariagemarriage.

Furthermore, though one of them should hauehave a disease, which is continuallcontinual without intermission, & yet curable, or any other incōuenienceinconuenienceinconvenience should befall either of them, after the sure-making, wherbywhereby they become lame, deafedeaf,
or dumbedumb, &c. yetYet this is not a sufficient cause to mouemove them to renounce, and dissoluedissolve the contract.

A second Casecase. What if it falleth out, that after the finishing of the contract, one of the espoused persons beebe long absent from the other, so as the absence beebe preiudiciallprejudicial to the mariagemarriage, that should ensue vponupon the contract?
Answ. InquirieInquiry must be made, whether this absence be voluntarievoluntary, or against the will of the partieparty.

If it be voluntarievoluntary. For example; if the man vponupon an honest and iustjust cause, the woman also being priuieprivy thereunto, shall go beyond seas, and being admonished of his dutieduty before hand, shalshall notwithstanding stay a whole yeareyear or more, and will not returnereturn, but further wilfully absent himselfehimself; then may it be lawfulllawful to the woman, to crauecrave of the publikepublic Magistrate a dissolution of the couenantcovenant made, & consequently marry another man, vnlesseunless the former, to whom she was contracted, be heard of. If he be, then shall it be lawfulllawful for him to pleadeplead for himselfehimself, and tendringtendering no
iustjust cause of his refusallrefusal, he shall be forced by the Magistrates authoritieauthority to stand to his promise, and take the woman for his wife. And the same order is to be taken in the wilfullwilful absence of the woman, after she is contracted.

If againeagain, the man or woman shall vponupon an euillevil mind, and with purpose to deceiuedeceive each other, absent thēseluesthemseluesthemselves, and depart; meanesmeans must be vsedused, that they may be admonished of their dutieduty. That being done, or at least vndertakenundertaken, and yet the partieparty offending will not appeareappear, if the other that is present, vponupon certainecertain knowledge of his, or her want in respect of continenciecontinency, shall sue to the Magistrate; after publikepublic and solemnesolemn notice giuengiven, the contract may be broken.

But if on the other side, either of them be absent against their wilwill, and intendeth no fraud or deceit, but is violently detained, by captiuitiecaptivity, imprisonment, sicknessickness, force, banishment, transportation or such like; then the partieparty present being desirous of the consummation of the mariagemarriage, ought either to
make meanesmeans vntounto him, and expect his returnereturn, or hauehave certainecertain notice of his death, before she promise, or hauehave to do with any other in way of mariagemarriage.
A third Casecase. What if after the contract, one of the parties becomes furious, or maddemad?

Answ. If the disease be continuallcontinual, without intermission, in all equitieequity and likelihood, the espousals are to be dissolueddissolved, vnlesseunless both parties after knowledge and experience of the disease, hauehave knowneknown one another: yet in this, and all such like cases, it is fit that all good meanesmeans be tried and vsedused, and sufficient time be giuengiven for the restoring of the diseased, to their former good estate, and for the accomplishment of the mariagemarriage lawfully begun, as before.

div.head: CHAP. 8.
Of MariageMarriage.
div.p:
MAriageMarriage is that, wherbywhereby the coniunctionconjunction formerly begunnebegun in the contract, is solemnelysolemnly manifested, and brought to perfection.
MariageMarriage is consummate by three sorts of actions; one of the parents of the Bridebride and BridegroomeBridegroom, the other of the Minister in publikepublic, the third of the persons coupled together.

The action of the Parentsparents is vponupon the Mariagemarriage-day, to bring the Bridebride, and deliuerdeliver her to the Bridebride-groomegroom, that they two may become actually man and wife, and performeperform each to other all matrimoniallmatrimonial duties.

And where the mariagemarriage is complete, in any other manner, so as the Parentsparents vponupon sound iudgementjudgement and deliberation, shall deny their full and free consent, either in expresseexpress words, or by cōniuenceconniuenceconnivence and silence, and that vponupon iustjust and lawfulllawful cause; there, though in the ciuillcivil courts of men, it may stand, and the children borne therein beebe legitimate before men, yet the truth is, before God it is of no force, but a meeremere nullitienullity.

And because this doctrine, touching consent of parents in these Cases, is of great vseuse, and auailethavaileth much to the supporting and mainta ••• ining of families; I
will first open the truth thereof, and then proueprove it by reasons.

VnderUnder the name of parents are comprehended; First, the Father and Mothermother. Secondly, all Tutors and Guardians, who hauehave the proper & sole charge of wards, or others vnderunder yearesyears of discretion. Thirdly, all such as are kindred of blood, who are in stead of parents to childrēchildren, as the vncleuncle by the fathers side, the vncleuncle by the mothers side, and such like.

Now touching the consent of parents, that is, of father and mother, I hold it requisite of necessitienecessity to marriage: For the authoritieauthority of parents must not be resisted, or violated. As for Tutors, and such as hauehave the place of parents, their consent is not required of necessitienecessity, butDe honestate. of honestiehonesty at least, because the power and authoritieauthority of the parent, though it be not taken away, yet it is lessened, when it is either transferred to another person, or in part resteth in the child alreadiealready bestowed.

Secondly, by parents consent, I vnderstandunderstand that which they giuegive, not
rashly, vnaduisedlieunadvisedly, or foolishliefoolishly, but out of good & wise consideration, and vponupon true and sound iudgementjudgement, of the businessebusiness in hand: For otherwise, as much as in them lieth, they make the mariagemarriage void and of none effect. And they are then thought to carriecarry a right iudgementjudgement of the thing, when they be able to yeeldyield a iustjust cause of yeeldingyielding, or denying their consent. For example; if a father denies to bestow his daughter IuliaJulia vponupon Sempronius, because heehe knowesknows him to be an Arrian, a Pelagian, or of any other sort of HeretikesHeretics; he withholdeth his consent vponupon a good ground, & he doth that which he doth, of iudgementjudgement.

Yet further I addeadd, that where the parents do dissent, and can yeeldyield no probable cause thereof; the mariagemarriage consummate without their consent, ought to be confirmed and ratified by the authoritieauthority of the Magistrate, who is Pater patriae. And this seemesseems to be the most equallequal course, both for the auoidingavoiding of greater scandals, & for the preuentingpreventing of wrong, that may otherwise
be done in some particular case, as to a woman that is defloureddeflowered and reiectedrejected.

Thirdly, consent of parents is either expressed, or implied; Expressed, when it is giuengiven by words; Implied, when it is yeeldedyielded by silence. For it standeth with most equitieequity and indifferencieindifferency, to thinkethink that those parents do giuegive consent, who do not by word expreslyexpressly deniedeny the same.

Fourthly, children are either subiectsubject to the authoritieauthority of their parents in the familiefamily; or at their owneown libertieliberty, & out of their parents subiectionsubjection. Those that are at liberty, are tied necessarily to subiectionsubjection in respect of mariagemarriage; but the other being still of the familiefamily, and vnderunder iurisdictionjurisdiction, are bound to be ordered, by their parents in the bestowing of themseluesthemselves.

This is briefly the meaning of the question in hand. Now, for proofeproof of this point, I will propound three sorts of arguments, wherofwhereof some are drawnedrawn from the law of God, some from the light of nature, and some from the iudgementjudgement of the ancient Church.

For the first sort. According to the law of God, mariagemarriage is not only a ciuillcivil and politikepolitic, but also a diuinedivine and spirituallspiritual coniunctionconjunction, the author and ordainer whereof, vponupon speciallspecial cause, was God himselfehimself: This our SauiourSaviour Christ witnesseth, when he saith, Those whom God hath ioynedjoined together, let no man separate, Matth. 19. 6. That therefore mariagesmarriages may be soundly ratified and confirmed, the authoritieauthority and power of God himselfehimself is necessarily to be interposed.
If it be asked, How God that is in heauenheaven, should bring and ioynejoin together man and wife vponupon the earth?

I answereanswer, that he doth it not immediately by himselfehimself, as he brought EuahEve vntounto Adam, but in & by some solemnesolemn and lawful meanesmeans. And this meanemean, is that great and ancient power and prerogatiueprerogative of parētsparents. And the law of God hath giuengiven them this power, not in ciuillcivil contracts and compositions alone, but eueneven in the beginning and accomplishing of mariagesmarriages. Deut. 7. 3. Thou shalt not giuegive thy daughter vntounto his sonneson,
nor take his daughter vntounto thy son. IeremJerem. 29. 6. Take wiueswives for your sonnessons, and giuegive your daughters vntounto husbands, that they may bearebear sonnessons and daughters. 1. Cor. 7. 36. But if any man thinkethink that it is vncomlieuncomely for his virgin, if sheeshe passepass the flower of her age, and need so require, let him doedo what he will, he sinneth not, let them be mariedmarried.

Hence it was, that Abraham by right of this authoritieauthority, gauegave order what wife his seruantservant should prouideprovide for his son; Thou shalt not take a wife to my sonneson of the daughters of the Canaanites; But thou shalt go vntounto my countriecountry, and to my kindred, and take a wife vntounto my sonneson Isaac, Gen. 24. 3. 4. SampsonSamson, though he was inflamed with the louelove of the womāwoman in Timnath, whom he saw to be beautifullbeautiful in his eyes, yet heehe durst not take her to his wife, till she was giuengiven him of his parents, IudgJudg. 14. It was an expresseexpress law of God, that if a man intisedenticed a maid that was not betrothed, and lay with her, heehe should endow her, and take her to his wife: But how? markeMark in what manner the holy Ghost proceedeth, If her father refuse
to giuegive her to him, he shall pay money according to the dowriedowry of virgins, Exod. 22. 16. 17. Deut. 22. 28. 29. In which text, Moses plainly teacheth, that the consent of the two parties is not sufficient, no not though they hauehave had societiesociety together, vnlesseunless they hauehave the free cōsentconsent of their parents also. In like manermanner it was ordained by God, Numb. 30. 4. 5. 6. That if a woman vowed a vow vntounto the Lord, being in her fathers house, & her father hearing it, holdeth his peace concerning her, that is, approuethapproves her vow by winking at it, her vow shall stand. But if her father disallow her, that is, giuethgiveth no approbation or consent vntounto the vow made, it shall be of no value, and the Lord wilwill forgiueforgive her, because her father consented not. Now, if the vow of children made vntounto God, and pertaining to his worship, cannot be ratified without the parents approbation; of how much lesseless force shall any priuateprivate contract or mariagemarriage be, without their allowance?

The second argument is taken from the light of nature, and it is gathered by proportion on this manner: A son priuilieprivily
alienateth and selleth away his fathers lands, either in whole or in part. The question is, whether this alienation be good in law, yea or no? AnswereAnswer is, No. And why? Because the land did not belong to the son, but was part of his fathers substance. In like manner, a son alienates himselfehimself, and is betrothed to a woman, to marriemarry her without his parents knowledge: Is this act of the son warrantable and sound? By no meanesmeans; for the son in respect of his body, is part of the fathers goods, and may not be alienated from him without consent. A notable reason hereof we find in IobJob 1. For when God had giuengiven Satan power to destroy and spoilespoil all IobsJobs goods, and whatsoeuerwhatsoever he had, the diuelldevil doth not only touch the wealth of IobJob, but his children also, as a part of his substance. In this respect the IewesJews were permitted by God to sell their children. Exodus 21. 7.

AgaineAgain, for the accomplishment of mariagemarriage, there must needs be a mutuallmutual donation, betweenebetween the spouse and the espoused. And what is that which is
mutually giuengiven? Surely their persons, or rather their bodies each to other, for so Paul saith, 1. Cor. 7. 2. Let eueryevery man hauehave his wife, and let eueryevery woman hauehave her owneown husband. But by whom is this donation to be made? byBy sons and daughters that are in the familiefamily, vnderunder the iurisdictionjurisdiction of their parents? It may not be; For nature her selfeself taketh it for granted, that he which is not at his own libertieliberty, cannot yeeldyield to the giuinggiving of himselfehimself. The donation therefore remainesremains in the right of the parent, in as much as the wilwill & consent of the child, ought to depend vponupon his wilwill and consent, to whom God hath giuengiven power and authoritieauthority in this behalfebehalf.

In the third place, let the iudgementjudgement of the ancient Church be obseruedobserved. Ambrose, in his first bookebook of the Patriarch Abraham, chap. 9. requiresRequires this consent in mariagesmarriages, which he saith is so equallequal and agreeable to nature, that euēeueneven the Poets acknowledged the same. For which purpose he reciteth two verses out of the Grecian Poet Euripides, in his TragedieTragedy called Andromacha, wherinwherein
in when Orestes desired to marriemarry Hermion, she frames him this answereanswer, That the matter of her mariagemarriage wholly depended vponupon the pleasure and authoritieauthority of her father, & was not in her owneown power or libertieliberty. Innocentius, who was both a Pope and Martyr, in his decretalldecretal epistles, so strictly requireth consent of parents,Sub Innocent. 3. canon. 51. as where it is wanting, he concludes the mariagemarriage to be void. In the CoūcellCouncellCouncil of Lateran, it was decreed that Clandestine contracts & secret mariagesmarriages, made and vndertakenundertaken betweenebetween partieparty and partieparty, should be holden as vnlawfullunlawful as mariagesmarriages in those degrees of consanguinitieconsanguinity and affinitieaffinity, which are forbidden by God. Tertullian saith,Tertul. lib. ad vxorem, 2. ad finem. That in this world the sonneson cannot Ritè & Iure. Basil. epist. 1. ad Amphiloch. Canon, 42. rightly and lawfully marriemarry without the allowance of his father. Basil in an Epistle to Amphilochius Bishop of Iconium, affirmeth; That mariagesmarriages which are made without them which hauehave power ouerover the parties, are fornications, and therefore that they which are ioynedjoined together in mariagemarriage, while their parents or masters liuelive, are in no sort free from imputation of sin, vntilluntil they hauehave approbation from them, for then
mariagemarriage is ratified & confirmed, when they hauehave yeeldedyielded allowance thereunto.

The second Action touching the consummation of mariagemarriage, is the action of the Minister. And that is the blessing or sanctification thereof, which is a solemnesolemn workework, wherbywhereby the Minister pronouncing the parties contracted to be man and wife before the whole congregation, commendeth them and their estate vntounto God by solemnesolemn prayer.

This solemnesolemn sanctification is grounded vponupon the practise of God himselfehimself, who hauinghaving giuengiven EuahEve to Adam, blessed them, saying, Increase and multipliemultiply, Gen. 2. 22. andAnd 1. 27. For that which God then gauegave, the Minister standing in his roomeroom, now prayeth may be giuengiven to the man and wife. Yea it is agreeable to the generallgeneral rule of the Apostle, Let all things beebe done decently and in order, 1. Cor. 14. 40.
Now that this action is to be approuedapproved and vsedused in the Church, appearesappears by these reasons.

list.item:
I. MariageMarriage as it is a publikepublic action, so it is after a sort a spirituallspiritual and diuinedivine ordinance, whereby it
differeth from the contract: For the contract being meerelymerely ciuillcivil, as it standeth by consent of men, so by the same consent, it may beebe broken and dissolueddissolved, but with mariagemarriage it is otherwise.
II. Marriage is the SeminarieSeminary of the Church and Commoncommon-wealth.

III. It was the practise of yethe PrimitiuePrimitive Church. Tertullian speaking of the marriage of Christians with Christians,Lib. 2. ad vxorem. acknowledgeth himselfehimself not to beebe able sufficiently to declare the happineshappiness of that coniunctionconjunction which is made by the Church, consecrated by prayers & Oblationem sic exponit Beatus Rhenanus. Niceph. lib. 14. cap. 55. Ambros. epistolar. lib. 9. epist. 70. ad Vigilium. solemnesolemn seruiceservice, witnessed by the Angels, and ratified by God himselfehimself. Nicephorus reporteth of one Synesius, who auouchedavouched that God & the laweslaws, and the holy hand of Thesphylus had giuengiven him a wife. Ambrose saith, That mariagemarriage ought to be sāctifiedsanctified, with the vaileveil wherewith the Priest was wont to couercover the Bridebride and the Bridebride-groomegroom in the publikepublic congregation, and with his blessing.

div.p:
The third and last action belonging to the accomplishment of this estate, is, that of the parties themseluesthemselves, whereby the Bridebride is in decent and modest manner,
brought vntounto the house and home of the Bridebride-groomegroom. It is the law of this estate published by God himselfehimself in Paradise, that the man, eueneven in respect of habitation, should leaueleave father and mother and cleauecleave to his wife, Gen. 2. 24,

HeereHere question is mouedmoved, whether mariagemarriage is to be solemnized with mirth and feasting. Answ. I. It is lawfulllawful and warrantable to vseuse feasting and mirth at mariagesmarriages, because these be things indifferent, and weewe hauehave examples thereof in the Scriptures. Laban made a feast at the wedding of IacobJacob and Rachel, and inuitedinvited all the men of the place to it, Gen. 29. 22. Christ himselfehimself did approueapprove the resort of people to the mariagemarriage at Cana in Galilee, both by his presence, and by that honorable gift of sixesix water-pots of the best wine, IohJoh. 2. 2. 7. 8. II. It is not only lawfulllawful, but conuenientconvenient and fit to be done, if there be abilitieability; according to the commendable customecustom of the place & countriecountry wherinwherein men do dwell; so as in the vseuse thereof, these cautions beebe obseruedobserved. First, that in mirth and merry-making, there
be care had that nothing be done which is dishonest, prophaneprofane, or of ill report. Philip. 4. 8. WhatsoeuerWhatsoever things are honestpurehonest, pure, of good report, thinkethink on these things. Secondly, That ioyjoy in them be mixed and moderated with the fearefear of God, without which Laughter and reioycingrejoicing is meeremere madnessemadness, Eccles. 2. 2. Thirdly, That it beebe performed in a moderate and sober vseuse of the creatures, without riot & excesseexcess. Thus we readeread that at the great feast of Ahashuerosh, it was appointed by the King himself, that they should drink orderly, & none might compel another to drinkedrink more then he thought conuenientconvenient, EsterEsther 1. 8. And where weddings are kept contrary to these directions, they are not feasts celebrated vntounto God, but vntounto yethe diuelldevil; which also may be said of all other festiuallfestival meetings.

And so much touching the point of mariagemarriage, in which this is to be remembredremembered for a cōclusionconclusion, That where there is generally a nullitienullity in the contract, or a separation following vponupon it, there is also a nullity in regard of the consummation of mariagemarriage.

div.head: CHAP. 9.
Of the dutiesDuties of marriedMarried personsPersons.
div.p: THusThus farrefar hauehave we proceeded in the doctrine of marriage; and now we come to the duties which they who beebe mariedmarried are to performeperform each to other.
These are principally two: Cohabitation, and Communion.

Cohabitation is their quiet and comfortable dwelling together in one place, for the better performance of mutuallmutual duties. 1. Cor. 7. 10. And to the married command I, not I but the Lord, let not the wife separate her selfeself from her husband: vers. 12. But to the remnant I say, not the Lord, If any brother hauehave an vnbeleeuingunbelieving wife, and she be content to dwell with him, let him not forsake her: vers. 13. And the wife which hath an vnbeleeuingunbelieving husband, which is content to dwell with her, let her not forsake him. 1. Pet. 3. 7. Likewise let the men dwell together, as becōmethbecommethcometh them that
hauehave knowledge; giuinggiving honor to the woman as to the weaker vessellvessel, eueneven as they which are heiresheirs together of the grace of life, that your prayers be not interrupted.

This dutieduty must beebe kept especiallieespecially the first yeareyear of mariagemarriage, Deut. 24. 5. When a man taketh a wife, heehe shall not go on warfare, neither shall be charged with any businesbusiness, but shall beebe free at home one yeareyear, & reioycerejoice with his wife which he hath taken. And the ground of this commandementcommandment, no doubt, is, that they might learnelearn to know one anothers cōditionsconditions, and that they might workework a setledsettled affection one towards another, which afterward vponupon no occasion might beebe changed.

Yet they may beebe absent each from other in two cases: First, vponupon mutuallmutual consent for a time, for the performing of some businesbusiness, that is requisite for the familiefamily, ProuProv. 7. 19. For mine husband is not at home, he is gone a far iourneyjourney: at the appointed time he will returnereturn againeagain. Secondly, the like absence is allowed, when some great and weightieweighty affairesaffairs either in the Church or Commoncommon-wealth
