are in hand, 2. Sam. 11. 9. 10. But VriahUriah slept at the dooredoor of the Kings Palace, with all the seruantsservants of his Lord, and went not downedown to his house? v. II. Then VriahUriah answered DauidDavid; The ArkeArk, and Israel, and IudahJudah dwell in tents, and my Lord IoabJoab, and all the seruantsservants of my Lord abide in the open field; shall I then go into my house to eateeat, and drinkedrink, and lie with my wife? byBy thy life, and by the life of my soulesoul, I will not do this thing.

Hence ariseth a question: What if after mariagemarriage consummate, there grow vponupon one of the parties a contagious disease that cannot be cured, but is so lothsomeloathsome, that the other whole partieparty cannot endure cohabitation at all?

Answ. Both the mariagemarriage it selfeself, and the dutieduty of dwelling together, ought to continue firmefirm and sure notwithstanding: yet so as the sound partieparty neither may, nor ought in good conscience, to desire coniunctionconjunction with the other, whereby he, or she may bring infection vponupon themseluesthemselves, and consequently hurt their children, and indangerendanger the Commoncommon-wealth.
But if either of the parties hauehave not the gift of continenciecontinency, nor cannot abstaineabstain; they must sue for it vntounto God in earnest prayer, who will giuegive it vntounto them.
For there God hath called a man or woman to continenciecontinency, where they be necessarily hindredhindered from the vseuse of the ordinarieordinary and lawfulllawful remedieremedy of the contract.
The contrariecontrary to Cohabitation is Desertion.
Desertion is, when one of the married folkesfolks, vponupon a wilfullwilful, and obstinate mind of their owneown head, departeth from the other, without a iustjust, and necessarienecessary cause.
Touching this point, there beebe sundriesundry Cases expounded.

I. Case. Suppose that an husband which is an vnbeleeuerunbeliever, or an heretikeheretic in the foundation, of his owneown accord, vponupon detestation of true religion, quite forsakes the beleeuingbelieving wife, and denies any more to dwell with her; what is to be done?

Answ. All good meanesmeans must beebe
first vsedused to bring the infected partieparty to repentance; and when none will succeed, but the case remaineth desperate, then mariagemarriage is dissolueddissolved on his part, and the beleeuingbelieving wife is free to marriemarry another. So saith the Apostle, 1. Cor. 7. 15. If the vnbeleeuingunbelieving partieparty depart, let him depart; a brother or a sister is not in subiectionsubjection in such things; but God hath called vsus vntounto peace. In which words obserueobserve a twofold reason: I. He that is at libertieliberty may marriemarry another; now the beleeuingbelieving partieparty forsaken, is at libertieliberty; because heehe is not in subiectionsubjection in such things: therefore he may marriemarry another. II. God hath called vsus vntounto peace, saith Paul, and this peace cannot be kept, if the beleeuingbelieving partieparty forsaken cannot containecontain, vnlesseunless he marriemarry. Ambrose vponupon the place saith,Ambros. in 1. Cor. 7. 15. That mariagemarriage cannot stand firmefirm, which is separated from the worship and seruiceservice of God; and therefore it is no sinnesin in the partieparty that is for sakenshaken for Gods cause, to be married to another; and the vnbeleeuerunbeliever departing, sinneth both against God, and against the law of wedlock, because he denies to remain in that
estate, in regard of religion. Therefore heehe breakesbreaks the couenantcovenant of mariagemarriage, and the other is not bound in this case to keepekeep touch with him. Libr. 4. dist. 39. the master of the sentences, saith, That the beleeuingbelieving partieparty in this case, is not bound to follow the vnbeleeuerunbeliever when heehe departeth, but while heehe liueslives may marriemarry another. Lib. de Fide & operib. cap. 16 • 161•. Augustine affirmeth, that eueneven the wife which is ioynedjoined to her husband in lawfulllawful societiesociety, if sheeshe will not abide with her Christian husband, because he is a Christian, may be forsaken and left, without sin. And it is far better that the couenantcovenant should be dissolueddissolved, that man and wife hauehave made each with other, then that the CouenantCovenant which man hath made with God. The people of Israel being in affliction, were constrained to break the former made with strange women, that they might keepekeep the latter, Ezra 10. 11. 19.

It is alledgedalleged, that the vnbeleeuingunbelieving partieparty may haply repent, and then to make a dissolution is in vainevain. But I say, that it is as likely that he will neuernever repent, and therefore there is cause that the knot should be dissolueddissolved.

AgaineAgain, it is lawfulllawful (say some) to make a diuorcedivorce out of the case of AdulterieAdultery. Answ. The belieuingbelieving partieparty which is forsaken, is not the cause of the diuorcedivorce, but is a patient of the separation, wrongfully made by the vnbeleeuerunbeliever. And Christ where he mentioneth the Casecase of AdulterieAdultery, Matth. 19. speakethSpeaketh of an equallequal mariagemarriage, whereas Paul speakesspeaks of an vnequallunequal.
II. Case. What if there fall out a desertion betweenebetween two married folkesfolks, which are both beleeuersbelievers?

Answ. The faultiefaulty person, who is the cause of this desertion, is to be forced by course of CiuillCivil, and EcclesiasticallEcclesiastical censure, to performeperform his, or her dutieduty. VponUpon which proceeding, if he remaineremain obstinate and peruerseperverse in will; the other must in patience, & earnest prayer vntounto God, waitewait the time, vntilluntil his mind may be changed, and he made to relent by the order of the Magistrate. But if the one of them, by iustjust occasion of fearefear, be compelled to depart from the other; and cannot returnereturn againeagain without apparent danger of life; in this
case they are not bound to returnereturn; but the delinquent partieparty is to remaineremain solitariesolitary, till they be instructed and made willing to doedo their duties: and in the meanemean while, the partieparty innocent must be resoluedresolved that God hath called him or her to single life.

AgaineAgain, be it that the one is resolutely vnwillingunwilling to dwell with the other, and thereupon flies away without any fault of the other; if the thing after a long space beebe sufficiently knowneknown before-hand, and all possible meanesmeans hauehave been vsedused, to reclaimereclaim the guiltieguilty person; yea being called, he doth not personally appeareappear before the IudgeJudge, to yeeldyield a reason of the fact; after publikepublic and solemnesolemn declaration made, the Minister vponupon such desertion, may pronounce the mariagemarriage to be dissolueddissolved. For he that vponupon malice flieth away from his mate, is to beebe holden in the same termesterms with an vnbelieuerunbeliever, who departs vponupon detestation of religion, and the seruiceservice of God, 1. Tim. 5. 8.

Howbeit, if the place whither he is fled, be vnknowneunknown, and vponupon his flight
there be found some fault in the PlaintiffePlaintiff, she is not to be heard, or set at libertieliberty by the IudgeJudge in this case, though sheeshe pretend want of the gift of continenciecontinency.

But suppose he that fled come againeagain vnlookedunlooked for, and requires his spouse; then in case the former course hath not binbeen taken, nor iudgementjudgement giuengiven against him, they may be reconciled and come together againeagain. If it hath, and matters be concluded, heehe is not vponupon his returnereturn to beebe heard, but rather seuerelyseverely punished.
Like vntounto Desertion, is malicious and spitefullspiteful dealing of married folkesfolks one with the other.

Malicious dealing is, when dwelling together, they require each of other intolerable conditions: and when the one doth not regard nor relieuerelieve the other, being in danger or extremity, as is meet. For this is as much as to betray one anothers estate and life to their vtterutter enemies.

HeereHere it may be demanded, what a belieuerbeliever should do, who is in certainecertain
and imminent danger, either of losseloss of life, or breach of conscience, if they both abide together?

Answ. I. This certainecertain danger hath his originalloriginal, either from one that is a stranger, or from one of the parties: If from a stranger, then the husband either takes vponupon him the defence of his belieuingbelieving wife, or not; if he doth, then she ought to abide with him. If not, she may depart and prouideprovide for her owneown safetiesafety. II. AgaineAgain, if the husband threatneththreateneth hurt, the belieuingbelieving wife may fliefly in this case; and it is all one, as if the vnbelieuingunbelieving man should depart. For to depart from one, and driuedrive one away by threats, are aequipollent.

Neither may this seemeseem strange vntounto any, that the belieuerbeliever in such case is allowed to depart. For a husband that is a Christian is married two waiesways: First with Christ, and secondly with his wife. The former mariagemarriage is made in Baptismebaptism, and is a more holy coniunctionconjunction, then is the latter. TherforeTherefore when these two cannot stand together, but one of them must needs be dissolueddissolved; the latter
must rather be left then the former. AgaineAgain, if the belieuerbeliever should remaineremain with the vnbelieuerunbeliever, she should hapliehaply be vrgedurged sometimes, in case of danger vponupon infirmitieinfirmity, to deny Christ, & make ship wrackewrackshipwreck of faith and good conscience; which may in no sort be done of either partieparty: and therefore separation is to be made rather in this society, then that the cōiunctionconiunctionconjunction with Christ should not stand firmefirm, and continue.
It is alledgedalleged, that if this be so, then the belieuingbelieving wife forsakes the vnbelieuingunbelieving husband, which she may not do.

Answ. She forsakes him not finally, but leauesleaves him for a time. AgaineAgain, the desertion is not made by the person, which giuethgiveth place for the time, but by him in whom is the cause of the desertion; eueneven as he is not to be termed a SchismatikeSchismatic, which separateth himself, but heehe in whom is the cause of the SchismeSchism.
AgaineAgain, it is obiectedobjected, that he which flieth leauesleaves his calling; and eueryevery man must abide in his calling; according to the rule of the Apostle, 1. Cor. 7. 20.

Answ. There is a double calling; The generallgeneral, standing in the worship of God; The particular, as the calling of mariagemarriage, or of single life. When these two callings cannot stand together, the latter must giuegive place to the former, Luk. 14. 26. If any man come to me, & hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters; yea and his owneown life also, he cannot be my disciple.
III. Case. When the husband is perpetually absent from the wife, what is to be done?

Answ. If he be absent either because he is in captiuitiecaptivity, or vponupon malice, or fearefear, or any such like cause; the wife must rest in expectation of his returnereturn, till she hath notice of his death, either by sufficient testimonietestimony, or by apparantapparent likelihoods. Now in the want of testimonies, and coniecturesconjectures in this behalfebehalf, if the partieparty forsaken cannot certainly determine, that the absence was made vponupon an euillevil mind; some hauehave thought that it behouethbehoveth her to expect his commingcoming again for the space of fourefour years; others of fiuefive; some of seuenseven, some of
ten yearesyears; after which time, she is free, and may marriemarry another man. And if the partieparty do hapliehaply returnereturn againeagain after some long space of time, who was probablieprobably thought to hauehave been dead, the latter mar • iagemarriage vndertakenundertaken vponupon necessarienecessary ignorance of such an euentevent, may be dissolueddissolved; and it shall not be imputed to either partieparty, considering it fell out not by their fault, but only by accident.
Now if the question beebe of wilfullwilful and affected absence, the same is to be determined concerning that, which hath binbeen said before touching the point of Desertion.

div.head: CHAP. 10.
Of the Communion of married folkesfolks, and of due beneuolencebenevolenceMarried Folks.
div.p:
THeThe cōmunioncommunion of man & wife, is that dutieduty, whereby they do mutually and willingly communicate, both their persons, & goods each to other, for their mutuallmutual helpehelp,
necessitienecessity and comfort, Ephes. 5. 28. So ought mēmen to louelove their wiueswives as their own bodies; he that louethloveth his wife, louethloveth himselfehimself.

This dutieduty consisteth principally in the performance of special beneuolēcebeneuolencebenevolence one to another, & that not of courtesiecourtesy, but of due debt, 1. Cor. 7. 3. Let the husband giuegive vntounto the wife due beneuolencebenevolence, and likewise also the wife vntounto the husband.
Due beneuolencebenevolence must be shewedshowed with a singular and entire affection one towards another; and that three waiesways principally.
First, by the right and lawfulllawful vseuse of their bodies, or of the marriage-bed, which is indeed an essentiallessential dutieduty of mariagemarriage.
The mariagemarriage-bed signifieth that solitariesolitary and secret societiesociety, that is betweenebetween man and wife alone.

And it is a thing of it owneown nature indifferent; neither good nor bad; and so Paul numbereth it amongst indifferent things, 1. Cor. 7. 27. Art thou bound vntounto a wife? seekeSeek not to be loosed: art thou loosed from a wife? seekeSeek not a wife. WherforeWherefore the Church of Rome erreth two
contrariecontrary waiesways. First, in that it maketh mariagemarriage to be a Sacramentsacrament, and so euerieevery action of it, to be of the owneown nature good. Secondly, in that they prohibiteprohibit mariagemarriage of certainecertain parties, and the reason of the prohibition may seemeseem to be this; that they thinkethink this secret commingcoming together of man and wife to be filthinesfilthiness.Canon. Proposuisti, Distinct. 82. This was the sentence of Syricius, that filthiefilthy Pope of Rome; who determined that mariagemarriage was the vncleannesseuncleanness of the flesh, and to that purpose abused the words of the Apostle, Rom. 8. 8. affirmingAffirming, that they which are in the flesh, that is, in the estate of MatrimonieMatrimony, cannot please God. Yea and after that mariagemarriage was condemned by them, some began to detest and hate women,Sozomen. lib. 3. cap. 16. as Ephraim the Syrian,Sess. 8. Canon. 9. 10. of whōwhom EcclesiasticallEcclesiastical stories make mention. And the CouncellCouncil of Trent is of the same iudgementjudgement. For whereas it opposeth mariagemarriage and chastitiechastity; it plainly determineth that in mariagemarriage there is no chastitiechastity.

This commingcoming together of man and wife, although it be indifferent, yet by
the holy vsageusage thereof, it is made a holy and vndefiledundefiled action, Hebr. 13. 4. Mariagemarriage is honorable among all, and the beddebed vndefiledundefiled. And it is (as all other creatures and ordinances of God are) sanctified by the word & praierprayer, 1. Tim. 4. 3.—Forbidding to marry, &c. vV. 4.—And nothing ought to be refused:—for it is sanctified by the word of God, & praierprayer. In which place it is to be obseruedobserved, how the Apostle applieth the point of sanctification directly to mariagemarriage.

The word of God giuethgiveth direction to married folkesfolks two wayesways. First, by giuinggiving them warrant, that they may lawfully do this action; because whatsoeuerwhatsoever is not done of faith (which faith must be grounded on Gods word) is a sin. Secondly, by prescribing the right and holy manner of doing the same.
The holy manermanner stands in these particulars.

First, that it be done in moderation. For eueneven in wedlockewedlock excesseexcess in lusts is no better then plaineplain adulterieadultery before God.Ambros. lib. de Philosoph. citat. ab August. contr. Iulianum. lib. 2. This is the iudgementjudgement of the ancient Church, that Intemperance, that
is, immoderate desire eueneven betweenebetween man and wife, is fornication.
Secondly, that it be vsedused in an holy abstinence.
Abstinence from this secret societiesociety, must be vsedused in two cases.

First, while the woman is in her flowers, LeuitLevit. 18. 19. Thou shalt not go to a woman to vncoueruncover her shame, as long as sheeshe is put apart for her disease. And it is made one of the properties of a good man, not to lie with a menstruous woman, Ezek. 18. 6.

Secondly, in the time of a solemnesolemn fast, when some grieuousgrievous calamitiecalamity is imminent. Then they are to giuegive themseluesthemselves (by mutuallmutual consent) to fasting and prayer, 1. Cor. 7. 5. Defraud not one another, except it be with consent for a time, that you may giuegive your seluesselves to fasting and prayer: and againeagain come together, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinencieincontinency. 2. Sam. 11. 11. Then VriahUriah answered DauidDavid, The ArkeArk, and Israel, and IudahJudah dwell intents: and my Lord IoabJoab, and the seruantsservants of my Lord abide in the open fields: shall I then go into mine house to eateeat and
drinkedrink, and lie with my wife? By thy life, and by the life of thy soulesoul, I will not do this thing. Zach. 12. 12. The familiefamily of the house of DauidDavid shall mournemourn apart, and their wiueswives apart; the familiefamily of the house of Nathan apart, and their wiueswives apart, &c.

Next vntounto the word, this action may be sanctified by prayer, for a blessing vponupon it. Children are the gift of God, and therforetherefore married folkesfolks are not only to vseuse the meanesmeans, but also to pray for the obtaining of them, Psal. 113. 9. He maketh the barren woman to dwell with a familiefamily, and to be a ioyfulljoyful mother of children. Psal. 127. 3. Behold children are the inheritance of the Lord, and the fruit of the wombewomb his reward. Examples for this purpose are these, Gen. 25. 21. Isaac prayed vntounto the Lord for his wife, because sheeshe was barren, and the Lord was intreatedentreated of him; and Rebekah his wife conceiuedconceived. 1. Sam. 1. 26. 27. And she said, Oh my Lord, as thy soulesoul liuethliveth, my Lord, I am the woman that stood with thee here, praying vntounto the Lord. vers. 27. I prayed for this child, and the Lord hath giuengiven me my desire, which I asked of him.

p.hi: Now the fruits, which are reaped and inioyedenjoyed by this holy vsageusage of the mariagemarriage bed, are three.

list.item: I. The hauinghaving of a blessed seed. Deut. 28. 1. If thou shalt obey diligently the voice of the Lord thy God, &c. Blessed shall be the fruit of thy bodiebody, and the fruit of thy ground. Which also is called the seed of God, being begot in an holy manermanner, Mal. 2. 15. And did not he make one? yetYet had he abundance of Spirit: And wherefore one? becauseBecause he sought a seed of God: therefore keepekeep your seluesselves in your spirit, and let none trespassetrespass against the wife of his youth.

II. The preseruationpreservation of the bodiebody in cleannessecleanness, that it may be a fit Temple for the holy Ghost to dwell in, 1. Thess. 4. 3. 4. This is the will of God, eueneven your sanctification, that eueryevery one of you should know how to possessepossess his vessellvessel in holinesholiness and honor, and not in the lust of concupiscence, eueneven as the Gentiles that know not God.

III. The holy estate of marriage is a liuelylively type of Christ and his Church, and this communion of married persons, is also a figure of the coniunctionconjunction that is betweenebetween him, and the faithfullfaithful, Hos. 2. 19. I will marriemarry
thee vntounto me, for euerever; yea I will marriemarry the vntounto me in righteousnesrighteousness, in iudgementjudgement, in merciemercy and in cōpassioncompassion: I will eueneven marriemarry thee vntounto me in faithfulnesfaithfulness, and thou shalt know the Lord. Ephes. 5. 23. For the husband is the wiueswives head, eueneven as Christ is the head of the Church, and the same is the SauiourSaviour of his bodiebody.

div.p: HeereHere some questions are to be resoluedresolved.
CaseCasecase. I. Whether may mariagemarriage be dissolueddissolved in the case of barrennessebarrenness?

Answ. No. For barrennessebarrenness is an hidden infirmitieinfirmity for the most part, and which God hath many times cured, eueneven when it seemed to be desperate, as in Sarah. Again, the fruit of the wombewomb is Gods blessing; and wholly dependeth vponupon him. HeeHe therefore that in want of children, reiectethrejecteth his wife, whom he hath receiuedreceived at the hands of God, offereth wrong eueneven to God himselfehimself.

CaseCasecase II. What if either of the married folkesfolks commit fornication, or any sinnesin of the same kind greater then fornication, as Incest, SodomieSodomy, lying
with beasts, or such like.

Answ. AdulterieAdultery and fornication are most grieuousgrievous and open crimes, which do breakebreak the very bond and couenantcovenant of mariagemarriage, ProuProv. 2. 17. andAnd therforetherefore when they are certainly knowneknown by such persons, they are at no hand to be winked at, but the Magistrate is presently to be informed of them. Howbeit, if the innocent partieparty be willing to receiuereceive the adulterer againeagain, in regard of his repentance; lest heehe should seemeseem to fauourfavour and maintainemaintain sin, and to beebe himselfehimself a practiser of vncleannesseuncleanness, he is to repairerepair to the Congregation, and declare the whole matter to the Minister, that he may vnderstandunderstand the parties repentance, and desire of forgiuenesseforgiveness.

And if the adulteresseadulteress hath conceiuedconceived, and is in trauelltravel, the husband to auoidavoid the imputation of hauinghaving an heireheir in bastardiebastardy, is to make relation to the Church of the repentance of the adulteresseadulteress; or to acquaint some certainecertain persons therewith, not to the end that she should be punished for the fact, but
that they may take notice of a child cōceiuedconceiuedconceived in adultery, whom afterward he may lawfully put off, as none of his.

The matter being knowneknown, the innocent partieparty may require a diuorcementdivorcement. For adulterieadultery is such a sin, as doth quite break off not only the vseuse, but the bond and couenantcovenant of mariagemarriage, Matth. 19. 9. I say therefore vntounto you, that whosoeuerwhosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for whoredomewhoredom, and marriemarry another, committethcommiteth adulterieadultery, &c. And yet the same bond may be continued, and grow vpup againeagain by the good will and consent of the partieparty innocent, and consequently they may be reconciled, and dwell together still. 1. Sam. 25. 44. Now Saul had giuengiven Michal his daughter DauidsDavids wife, to Phalti the sonneson of Laish, which was of Gallim. 2. Sam. 3. 14. Then DauidDavid sent messengers to Ishbosheth Sauls sonneson, saying, DeliuerDeliver me my wife Michal, which I married for an hundred foreskins of the PhilistimsPhilistines. The same course may be taken in like cases by the innocent, specially vponupon the repentance of the guiltieguilty person. But yet eueryevery man must be left
to his owneown conscience, and none is to beebe compelled to take another, from whom heehe may iustlyjustly beebe separated against his will.

Now in requiring of a diuorcedivorce, there is an equallequal right and power in both parties, so as the woman may require it as well as the man; and he as welwell as she. The reason is, because they are equally bound each to other, and hauehave also the same interest in one anothers bodiebody; prouidedprovided alwaiesalways, that the man is to maintainemaintain his superioritiesuperiority, and the woman to obserueobserve that modestiemodesty which beseemeth her towards the man.

After the diuorcementdivorcement made, it shalshall be lawful for the harmelesseharmless partieparty, not hauinghaving the gift of continenciecontinency, vponupon leaueleave obtained of the Church, and the Christian Magistrate, to marriemarry againeagain.
But what then shall become of the partieparty offending?

Answ. If vponupon the hazard of his Conscience in want of the remedieremedy, any libertieliberty of second mariagemarriage, beebe to beebe granted vntounto him by the Church or CiuillCivil Magistrate; (as indeed here in
England there is not;) diuersdivers restraints, in this Casecase, must be obseruedobserved.

First, no such libertieliberty is to be granted, so long as the matter remainesremains vncertaineuncertain, whether they may be reconciled, specially while the partieparty innocent liuethliveth in single life. Secondly, it must euidentlyevidently appeareappear, that the said offending partieparty hath earnestly rpentedrepented him of his sin, before he can either be receiuedreceived into the Church, or admitted to a second mariagemarriage. Thirdly, this liberty is not to be granted him either presently, or vnaduisedlyunadvisedly; but vponupon frequent and serious admonition, rather to giuegive himselfehimself to mourning and lamentation, and still to remaineremain alone, then to desire againeagain to enioyenjoy the benefit of that state, which he hath alreadiealready so shamefully abused.
So much of the first way of performance of due beneuolencebenevolence.

The second way is, by cherishing one another: Ephes. 5. 29. No man euerever hated his owneown flesh, but nourisheth and cherisheth it, as Christ also doth the Church. This cherishing is the performing of any duties,
that tend to the preseruingpreserving of the liueslives one of another. Wherefore they are freely to cōmunicatecommunicate their goods, their coūselcounsel, their labors each to other; for the good of themseluesthemselves and theirs.

The third way is, by an holy kind of reioicingrejoicing and solacing themseluesthemselves each with other, in a mutuallmutual declaration of the signessigns and tokens of louelove and kindnessekindness. ProuProv. 5. 18. ReioyceRejoice with the wife of thy youth: vers. 19. Let her be as the louingloving Hind, and pleasant wild goat: let her breasts satisfiesatisfy thee at all times, and delight in her louelove continually. Cantic. 1. 1. Let him kissekiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for thy louelove is better them wine. Gen. 26. 8. So after he had binbeen there a long time, AbimelekAbimelech King of the PhilistimsPhilistines, looked out at a window, and loelo, heehe saw IsaakIsaac sporting with Rebekah his wife: Then AbimelekAbimelech called IsaakIsaac and said; LoeLo, sheeshe is of a suretiesurety thy wife. Esay 62. 7. As a yongyoung man marrieth a virgin, so shall thy sonnessons marriemarry thee; and as a BridegroomeBridegroom is glad of the Bridebride, so shall thy God reioycerejoice ouerover thee.

This reioycingrejoicing and delight is more permitted to the man, then to the woman;
and to them both, more in their yongyoung yearesyears, then in their old age.

div.head: CHAP. 11.
Of the Husband.
div.p: MArriedMarried folkesfolks are either husbādhusband or wife.

The husband is he which hath authoritieauthority ouerover the wife; hereupon in Scripture he is called the guide of her youth, ProuProv. 2. 17. andAnd they twainetwain being but one flesh, he is also the head ouerover his wife.
The duties of the husband towards the wife, are these:

I. To louelove her as himselfehimself: Eph. 5. 33. Let eueryevery one louelove his wife eueneven as himselfehimself. Gen. 24. 67. Afterward IsaakIsaac brought her vntounto the tent of Sarah his mother; and heehe tooketook Rebekah and she was his wife, and he louedloved her: so IsaakIsaac left mourning for his mother. Note, how the louelove of the husband to the wife, mitigates sorrow for the death of the mother.

He is to shewshow this louelove in two things: First in protecting her from danger, Gen. 20. 16. And vntounto Sarah he said, behold I hauehave giuengiven 1000. shekelsShekels of siluersilver vntounto thy brother: behold he is the coueringcovering of thine eieseyes amongst all that are with thee. Let it be knowneknown amongst all, & be thou instructed. 1. Sam. 30. 5. DauidsDavids two wiueswives were taken prisoners also, Ahinoam the Izreelite, and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite: v. 8. Then DauidDavid asked counsellcounsel of the Lord saying; Shall I follow after this companiecompany,? shallShall I ouertakeovertake them? And heehe answered him, Follow, for thou shalt surely ouertakeovertake them, and recouerrecover all. Secondly, in regarding her estate as his owneown, and prouidingproviding maintenance for her, both for his life time, and as much as he may, for time to come after his death. Ephes. 5. 28. So ought men to louelove their wiueswives, as their owneown bodies: he that louethloveth his wife louethloveth himselfehimself; vers. 29. For no man yet hated his owneown flesh, but nourisheth it, &c. Exod. 21. 10. If he take him another wife, he shall not diminish her food, her raymentraiment, and recompencerecompense of her virginitievirginity. Ruth. 3. 9. VntoUnto whom he said, who
art thou? whichWhich said; I am Ruth thine handmaid, spread therefore the wing of thy garment ouerover thine handmaid; for thou art the kinsman.
II. To honor his wife: 1. Pet. 3. 7. GiuingGiving honor to the woman.

This honor stands in three things: First, in making account of her, as his companion, or yoke-fellow. For this cause, the woman, when she was created, was not takētaken out of the mans head, because she was not made to rule ouerover him; nor out of his feet, because God did not make her subiectsubject to him as a seruantservant; but out of his side, to the end that man should take her as his mate. SecōdlySecondly, in a wise & patiētpatient bearing or coueringcovering of her infirmities, as anger, waywardneswaywardness and such like, in respect of the weaknesweakness of her sexesex, 1. Pet. 3. 7. GiuingGiving honor to the woman, as vntounto the weaker vessellvessel, seeing yeeye are heiresheirs together of the grace of life, that your prayers beebe not hindredhindered. Thirdly, by suffering himselfehimself sometimes to be admonished or aduisedadvised by her. It was Gods commandementcommandment to Abraham concerning Sarah his
wife; Let it not be grieuousgrievous in thy sight for the child, and for thy bond-woman: in all that Sarah shall say vntounto thee, hearehear her voice; For in IsaakIsaac shall thy seed be called, Gen. 21. 12. Thus Elkanah was willing to subscribe vntounto his wife AnnaesAnna's aduiceadvice, for her tarrying at home till the child was weaned, 1. Sam. 1. 23. And Elkanah her husband said vntounto her, do what seemeth thee best: tarrietarry vntilluntil thou hast weaned him: only the Lord accomplish his word. Hereupon the Heathen Philosopher said,Arist. Ethic. lib. 8. That the master of the familiefamily exerciseth (after a sort) a power Tyrannical ouerover his seruantsservants, a power RegallRegal ouerover his children; because Kings are fathers of their CōmonCommoncommon-wealesweals: but in respect of his wife, he exerciseth a power AristocraticallAristocratic, not after his owneown will, but agreeable to the honor and dignitiedignity of the married estate; and consequently, that he ought not in modestiemodesty to challenge the priuiledgeprivilege of prescribing and aduertisingadvertising his wife in alall matters domesticalldomestic, but in some to leaueleave her, to her owneown will and iudgementjudgement.
HeereHere question is mouedmoved, whether the husband may correct the wife?

Answ. Though the husband be the wiueswives head, yet it seemeth he hath no power nor libertieliberty granted him in this regard. For we readeread not in the Scriptures, any precept or example to warrant such practise of his authoritieauthority. He may reprouereprove & admonish her in word only, if he seeth her in fault. For, thus we readeread, that IacobJacob censured his wife, being impatient, eueneven in anger, Gen. 30. 2. Am I in Gods stead, which hath withholden from thee, the fruit of the wombewomb? And IobJob reprouedreproved his wife, IobJob 2. 10. Thou speakest like a foolish woman. What? Shall we receiuereceive good at the hand of God, and not receiuereceive euillevil? But heehe may not chastise her either with stripes, or stroksstrokes. The reason is plaineplain; Wiueswives are their husbands mates; and they two be one flesh. And no man will hate, much lesseless beat his owneown flesh, but nourisheth and cherisheth it, Ephes. 5. 29. AgaineAgain, it is the commandementcommandment of God, that man should not trespassetrespass against the wife of his youth, Malac. 2. 15. ChrysostomeChrysostom saith,In 1. Cor. 11. Homil. 26. It is the greatest reprochreproach for any man, that can beebe, to beatebeat his wife. Plutarch in the
life of Cato the Censor, affirmeth, that he which smiteth his wife, doth all one, as if he should lay violent hands vponupon the sacred images of the gods, which was counted an high degree of offence among the Heathen.

It is alledgedalleged, Husbandshusbands are cōmandedcommanded so to louelove their wiueswives, as Christ doth his Church; now Christ chastiseth his Church, with strokes; & therefore so may the husband his wife. Answ. As Christ doth entirely louelove his Church, so heehe may also chastise the same, because heehe is not only the husband, but also absolute Lord and King of his Church: so is not the husband absolute ouerover the wife.

But his authority ouerover the wife, is after a sort ciuillcivil, as is the authoritieauthority of the Magistrate ouerover his people. Ans. It is not so. For the Magistrate hath in his hand the power of the sword, by which power he inflicteth punishment in case of offence. But the husband can challenge to himselfehimself no such power: L. Consensu. C. de diuortijs. 〈…〉 L. Consensu. C. de diuortijs.〈…〉 yea it is flatly forbidden in the CiuilCivil law, that he should scourge or strike his wife.

NeuerthelesseNevertheless, if she grow to extremities, and be desperately peruerseperverse, so as there be no hope of amendment; then the Magistrate may be informed, who to preuentprevent scandals, and to prouideprovide for publikepublic peace, both ought and may assigneassign vntounto her necessary correction, and punishment according to her desert. Now the husband that hath a wife so stubbornestubborn and peeuishpeevish, must bearebear it, if it may be borne, as the portion of his crossecross laid vponupon him by God. And in this case, if he be impatient, he may in some sort be pardoned and pitied, but he is not wholly to be excused.

div.head: CHAP. 12.
Of the Wife.
div.p: THeThe wife is the other married person, who being subiectsubject to her husband, yeeldethyieldeth obedience vntounto him.

Touching the subiectionsubjection of the wife, the word of God mētionethmentioneth it in sundriesundry places. Rom. 7. 2.
The woman which is in subiectionsubjection to the man, is bound by the law to the man, while he liuethliveth. Ephes. 5. 24. As the Church is in subiectionsubjection to Christ, eueneven so let the wiueswives beebe to their husbands in eueryevery thing. Colos. 3. 18. Wiueswives submit your seluesselves vntounto your husbands, as it is comely in the Lord. 1. Tim. 2. 12. I permit not a woman—to vsurpeusurp authoritieauthority ouerover the man. And it was a law established by God immediately after the falfall, Gen. 3. 16. VntoUnto the woman he said, I wilwill greatly increase, &c. and thy desire shalshall be subiectsubject to thine husband, and he shall rule ouerover thee. Indeed the daughter, according to the CiuillCivil law, eueneven when sheeshe is married isIn potestate patris. in the power of her father, and not of her husband. But this is directly against the law of Moses, and crosseth the law of Naturenature, LeuitLevit. 22. 12. 13. Numb. 30. 13.
Now the duties of the wife, are principally two.

The first is, to submit her selfeself to her husband; and to acknowledge and reuerencereverence him as her head in all things. Gen. 20. 16. Likewise Abimelech said vntounto Sarah; Behold thy brother, that is, thy
husband, whom thou callest thy brother, is the vaileveil of thine eyes to all that are with thee. As if he should say, Thy husband is thy head, and hath power ouerover thee, and thou oughtest to reuerencereverence him. For of ancient times, the wife was coueredcovered with a vaileveil in the presence of her husband, in token of subiectionsubjection to him. Thus Rebekah at the sight of IsaakIsaac tooketook a vaileveil, and coueredcovered her head therewith, Gen. 24. 65. 1. Cor. 11. 3. The man is the womans head. Ephes. 5. 22. Wiueswives submit your seluesselves vntounto your husbands, as vntounto the Lord; for the husband is the wiueswives head, eueneven as Christ is the head of his Church. The reason hereof is good. For the wife enioyethenjoyeth the priuiledgesprivileges of her husband, and is graced by his honor and estimation amongst men. His NobilitieNobility maketh her noble, though otherwise sheeshe is base and meanemean; as contrariwise, his basenessebaseness and low degree, causeth her, though sheeshe beebe by birth noble and honorable, to beebe by estate base and meanemean.

The second dutieduty is, to be obedient vntounto her husband in all things; that is,
wholly to depend vponupon him, both in iudgementjudgement and will. For lookelook as the Church yeeldsyields obedience to Christ her head, and yeeldsyields her selfeself to be commanded, gouernedgoverned, and directed by him, so ought the woman to the man. So Sarah is said to obey Abraham, and to giuegive him the termesterms of obedience, SheeShe called him Lord, or Sir, 1. Pet. 3. 6. Hence it followeth, that the woman is not to take libertieliberty of wandringwandering, and straying abroad from her owneown house, without the mans knowledge & cōsentconsent. 2. King. 4. 22. Then she called to her husband and said, Send with me, I pray thee, one of the yongyoung men, and one of the asses; for I will haste to the man of God, and come againeagain. AgaineAgain, that sheeshe is to follow her husband, when heehe flitteth or departeth from place to place, vnlesseunless heehe forsake either her or Christ. To this purpose Paul saith heehe had power to lead about a wife, being a sister, as well as the rest of the Apostles, 1. Cor. 9. 5. Thus Sarah went with Abraham into Egypt, Gen. 12. 11. andAnd out of Egypt, Gen. 13. 1. andAnd to Gerar to soiournesojourn there, Gen. 20. 1. 2. 3. Thus
the wiueswives of IacobJacob departed with him, from their father Laban, Gen. 31. 17.

Contrary to these duties, are the sins of wiueswives; To be proud, to be vnwillingunwilling to bearebear the authority of their husbādshusbands; to chide and braulebrawl with bitternesbitterns; to forsake their houses, &c. ProuProv. 27. 15. A continuallcontinual dropping in the day of rainerain, and a contentious woman are alike. vers. 16. He that hideth her, hideth the windewind, & she is as the oyleoil in his right hand, that vtterethuttereth it selfeself. Exod. 4. 26. Then Zipporah said, O bloodiebloody husband; because of the Circumcision. It was the fault of the LeuitesLevites Concubineconcubine, IudgJudg. 19. 2. Who played the whore, and went away from him vntounto her fathers house to BethlemBethlehem IudahJudah, and there continued the space of fourefour monethsmonths. It was the sinnesin of QueeneQueen Vashi, who refused to come at the Kings word, which he had giuengiven in charge to the EunuchesEunuchs: therefore the King was verievery angrieangry, and his warthwrath kindled in him, EsterEsther 1. 12. Lastly, to be a cause of griefegrief to their kindred. Thus the proud wiueswives of Esau, the daughters of the Hittites, were a griefegrief of mind to IsaakIsaac and Rebekah, Gen. 26. 35. & 27. 46.

div.head: CHAP. 13.
Of the Parent.
div.p: HIthertoHitherto hath been treated of the first Couple, whereof the family cōsistethconsisteth, namely, of married folkesfolks. Now follow the other; and they are of two sorts; either such as, whereby the familiefamily is increased, and multiplied; or such as are helpeshelps thereunto.
Those whereby the familiefamily is inlargedenlarged, are also of two sorts; Parentsparents and Childrenchildren.
Parents are they which hauehave power and authoritieauthority ouerover children.
The duties of parents are especially two; One to bring vpup their children; The other to bestow them, when they hauehave brought them vpup.
Touching Educationeducation or bringing vpup of children, the parents care must beebe, both that they may liuelive, and also that they may liuelive well, Ephes. 6. 4.

Touching the preseruationpreservation of the life of the child, there are many duties
required of the Parentsparents, specially fourefour. First, the mother is her selfeself to giuegive the infant suckesuck, and to wrap it vpup in swadlingswaddling clothes. Paul cōmendscommends it for a note of a good wife, to nurse her owneown children, 1. Tim. 5. 10. Thus Sarah gauegave suckesuck to IsaakIsaac, Gen. 21. 7. Anna nursed Samuel, 1. Sam. 1. 22. DauidDavid in likelihood was nursed by his mother, Psal. 22. 9. Thou gauestgavest me hope eueneven at my mothers breasts. And our SauiourSaviour Christ was also nursed by MarieMary his mother, Luk. 11. 27. andAnd swadledswaddled, Luk. 2. 7. Now the reason hereof is plaineplain. God hath giuengiven milkemilk to women that bearebear children, & hath so appointed, that no meat is more naturallnatural to the child, then the mothers milkemilk. And nature it selfeself teacheth this in the course of other creatures. The earth nourisheth that which it bringeth forth. The fruit which the tree beareth is fed by the sap that comes from the root therofthereof. Yea amongst the bruit beasts, eueneven those that be most sauagesavage, as the TigresTigers, do giuegive suckesuck vntounto the yongyoung ones which they bring forth.

Yet in case of want of health, or abilitieability,
or any other iustjust impediment, the mother may in equity beforbornebe forborne, and the child committed vntounto a nurse. And so we readeread that Rebekah the daughter of Bethuel, and afterward the wife of IsaakIsaac had a nurse, Genes. 24. 59. whoseWhose name was Deborah, Gen. 35. 8. And Pharaohs daughter in a case of necessitienecessity, committed Moses to be nursed of an Hebrew woman, whom she tooketook not to be his mother, but a stranger; and her fact was allowed by God, Exod. 2. 7. 9.

The second dutieduty of the Parentparent is, to prouideprovide for his child meatemeat, drinkedrink, and clothing. Our SauiourSaviour Christ saith, that Parentsparents eueneven by the light of nature, though they be euillevil, will not deniedeny or withhold necessarienecessary food from their children: Mat. 7. 9. 10. What man is there among you, that if his son askeask him bread, will giuegive him a stone, or if he askeask a fish, will giuegive him a scorpion? And Paul saith, If there be any that prouidethprovideth not for his owneown, and namely for them of his housholdhousehold, heehe denieth the faith, and is worse then an InfidellInfidel, 1. Tim. 5. 8.

The third dutieduty is, when God giuethgiveth
abilitieability & meanesmeans, to lay vpup some thing for the future maintenance of the child. 2. Cor. 12. 14.—for the children ought not to lay vpup for the fathers, but the fathers for the children. ProuProv. 19. 14. House and riches are the inheritance of the fathers.

The fourth is, to obserueobserve both the inclination, and the naturallnatural gifts of bodiebody and mind that are in the child, and accordingly to bestow it in some honest calling & course of life. ProuProv. 20. 11. A child is knowneknown by his actions, whether his workework be pure and right. In the EcclesiasticallEcclesiastical historiehistory,Ruffin. Eccles. hist. lib. 1. c. 14. written by Ruffinus, it is recorded, that Alexander Bishop of Alexandria, saw a far off, in a place nearenear to the sea, a companiecompany of children playing together, and in their play imitating himselfehimself in sundriesundry MinisteriallMinisterial actions. And whēwhen he had a while viewed them, he perceiuedperceived that they examined & baptised one another, according to the solemnesolemn order vsedused in y•y•the CōgregationCongregation: which thing, whēwhen he had made some of his ClergieClergy acquainted withallwithal, and taken order that the children should be sent for, and brought before
him, he demanded of them, what sport they vsedused, and in what manner they played one with another. The children at first, for fearefear, denied what they had done, yet vponupon further examination they confessed, that they had made Athanasius (who afterward became Bishop of the place) their Bishop, and that heehe instructed and baptised sundriesundry of their companiecompany. He further asked both Athanasius himselfehimself, and those which were said to hauehave been baptised, what questions he asked them, and what answeresanswers they gauegave; and perceiuingperceiving by their speeches, that they had framed themseluesthemselves, though in sporting manermanner, to the Church-proceedings in those actions; vponupon conference had with his ClergieClergy, heehe determined, that those which had first been asked, and had giuengiven answereanswer fully, according to the formeform vsedused in that Church, and thereupon baptised, should not be rebaptised. And for Athanasius and the other children, which had done the part of Ministers in their kind, he sent for their parents, and gauegave them great charge
that they should be brought vpup in learning and religion, that so they might in time be fit for the publikepublic MinisterieMinistry. The like course we readeread to hauehave been taken by the Heathen, for iudgementjudgement of the inclination and towardnessetowardness of their children.Nazianz. epist. ad Eudoxam. The Athenians made a law, that before children were bestowed in any calling, they should beebe first brought into a publikepublic place, where Instruments belonging to all sorts of trades were laid; and look in what kind of Instrument any of them tooketook most delight, the child was thought to beebe most fit for the trade, whereunto that Instrument belonged, and afterward applied to the same with good successesuccess.

Now the Parentsparents first and principallprincipal care must be for the Church; that those of their children which hauehave the most pregnant wit, and be indued with the best gifts, be consecrated vntounto God, and brought vpup in the studiestudy of the Scriptures, to serueserve afterward in the MinisterieMinistry of the Church. Thus Anna dedicated Samuel her son vntounto God by vow, 1. Sam. 1. 11. And sheeshe vowed a vow, and
said, O Lord of HostesHosts, if thou wilt—giuegive vntounto thine handmaid a man-child, thēthen I wilwill giuegive him vntounto the Lord all the daiesdays of his life. And she did according to her vow, and the Lord blessed Samuel her sonneson, who in processeprocess of time became a great Prophet.
The next point of Educationeducation of children, is to prouideprovide that they may liuelive well, and lead a godly life. To this purpose Parentsparents must do three things.

First, they are to be carefullcareful, that the child, so soonesoon as may beebe, after it is borne, beebe admitted into the true Church of God by Baptismebaptism, and hauehave a fit name giuengiven vntounto it.

Secondly, they are to endeuourendeavour to sow the seeds of godlinessegodliness and religion in the heart of the child, so soonesoon as it comes to the vseuse of reason and vnderstandingunderstanding; and as it growesgrows in yearesyears, so care must be had that it grow in knowledge and grace. To this purpose is the vow and promise made in Baptismebaptism, which parents are bound to call vponupon the child to remember, when it comes to yearesyears. It was the godly care of Timothies
parents, 2. Tim. 3. 14. But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned, knowing of whom thou hast learned them, vers. 15. And that thou hast knowneknown the holy Scriptures of a child, which are able to make thee wise vntounto saluationsalvation, through the faith which is in Christ IesusJesus. This was the commandementcommandment of God to the parents of his people, Deut. 6. 7. Thou shalt rehearse these words which I command thee continually to thy children, and shalt talketalk of them whēwhen thou tarriest in the house. And vers. 20. When thy sonneson shall askeask thee in time to come, saying; What meanemean these Testimonies, and Ordinances, and LawesLaws, which the Lord our God hath commanded you? Then thou shalt say vntounto thy sonneson; We were Pharaohs bondmen in Egypt, &c. This was obseruedobserved by the Israelites in the ages su • cceeding: Psal. 44. 1. We hauehave heard with our earesears, O God: our fathers hauehave told vsus the workesworks that thou hast done in their daiesdays in old time.

Thirdly, the first instruction of children in learning & religion, must be so ordered, that they may take it with delight. For which purpose, they may be
sometimes allowed in moderate manermanner to play, and solace themseluesthemselves in recreatiōsrecreations fitting for their yearesyears. And if they do amisseamiss in either, they are to beebe restrained by the bridle of discipline. First by reproofereproof in word, and when that wilwill not helpehelp, by the rodderod of correction. Zach. 8. 5. The streets of the citiecity shall beebe full of boyesboys and girlesgirls, playing in the streets thereof. ProuProv. 29. 15. The rod and correction giuegive wisdomewisdom, but a child set at libertieliberty makes his mother ashamed. vers. 17. Correct thy son, and he will giuegive thee rest, and giuegive pleasures to thy soulesoul. Hebr. 12. 9. We hauehave had the fathers of our bodies which correct vsus, and we gauegave them reuerencereverence.

Yet in this point, two extreamesextremes are carefully to be auoidedavoided; That the Parentparent be not either too seueresevere, or too indulgent to the child. For seuer • itieseverity Paul giuesgives his rule, Ephes. 6. 3. Parentsparents prouokeprovoke not your children to anger, that is, by too much austeritieausterity in gouernmētgouernmentgovernment. For lenitielenity, we hauehave old Eli his example, 1. Sam. 2. 23. And he said vntounto them, Why do yeeye such things? forFor of all this people, I hearehear euillevil reports of you. DoeDo no more my
sonnessons, &c. So much for Educationeducation.

The second general dutieduty of parents, is the bestowing of their children; This bestowing is, when they knowing their children fit for mariagemarriage, not to hauehave the gift of continenciecontinency, do vseuse their best indeuourendeavour to prouideprovide matches for them in time, or at least, do aduiseadvise them theruntothereunto by themseluesthemselves or by their friends: 1. Cor. 7. 36. If any man thinkethink it vncomelieuncomely for his virgin to passepass the flower of her age, and need so require—let them beebe married. vers. 38. heHe that giuethgiveth her to mariagemarriage, doth well. IeremJerem. 26. 6. Take yeeye wiueswives—and take wiueswives for your sonnessons, and giuegive your daughters to husbands, &c. Gen. 28. 1. IsaakIsaac called IacobJacob and blessed him, and charged him and said vntounto him; Take not a wife of the daughters of Canaan: Arise, get thee to Padan Aram—and thence take thee a wife of the daughters of Laban thy mothers brother. IudgJudg. 14. 2. SampsonSamson came and told his father and his mother, and said, I hauehave seeneseen a woman in Timnah of the daughters of the PhilistimsPhilistines; now therefore giuegive me her to wife.

This dutieduty is now adaiesadays carelesselycarelessly
neglected of Parentsparents; and the fruit therofthereof is dangerous. For hence it comes to passepass, that their children oftentimes do either commit whoredomewhoredom, or vndertakeundertake wicked and vngodlyungodly mariagesmarriages.

In the choice of a husband or wife, the Parentsparents ought to hauehave a greater respect vntounto pietiepiety and wisedomewisdom, then vntounto beautiebeauty and riches, or any other outward blessings. Yet where they all concurreconcur, the partieparty so qualified is the more thankfully to be entertained. VponUpon these grounds the Priest of Prince of Midian, gauegave his daughter Zipporah to Moses, and Moses agreed to take her, Exod. 2. 19. A man of Egypt deliuereddelivered vsus from the PhilistimsPhilistines, and also drew vsus water enough, & watered the sheepesheep—And Moses agreed to dwell with the man, who gauegave vntounto Moses Zipporah his daughter. IosuJosu. 15. 16. Then Caleb said, He that smiteth Kiriath-sepher, and taketh it, eueneven to him will I giuegive Achsah my daughter to wife. Yea it is a sinnesin to marriemarry only for beautiebeauty, without consideration of the better things. Thus the old world sinned, whēwhen the sonnessons of God saw the daughters of men
that they were fairefair, and tooketook them wiueswives of all that they liked, Gen. 6. 2. andAnd SampsonSamson, who only vponupon the sight of the woman in Timnah, of the daughters of the PhilistimsPhilistines, without further inquirieinquiry, desired that she might be giuengiven him for his wife, IudgJudg. 14. 2.

AgaineAgain, it is meet that parētsparents should dealedeal moderately with their children in this case, and not vndertakeundertake at any hand to force and compel them to marriemarry this or that partieparty. This was the iustjust commendation of Rebekahs parents, who though they were Idolaters, yet had that regard of equity, that they first called her and asked her consent, before they sent her away with Abrahams seruantservant, to be mariedmarried to IsaakIsaac, Gen. 24. 58. Now in case the Parentsparents failefail in their dutieduty in this regard, the son or daughter may lawfully declare the matter first to their kinsfolkekinsfolk, and afterward (if need be) to the Minister, or Magistrate, and sue for redresseredress by their means and direction.

div.head: CHAP. 14.
Of the SonneSon.
div.p: THeThe sonneson is he, who is in subiectionsubjection to his parents.
The duties of a son to beebe performed to his parents, are principally two.

First to yeeldyield them obedience, whether they be his naturallnatural parents or otherwise, as his step-father & step-mother, and that while he liuethliveth. Eph. 6. 1. Children obey your parents in the Lord; for this is right. Luke 2. 51. Then heehe went downedown with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subiectsubject to them. Exod. 18. 19. Moses father in law said vntounto him, HeareHear now my voice, I will giuegive thee counsellcounsel, and God shall be with thee. Ruth 3. 5. And Ruth said vntounto Naomi her mother in law, All that thou biddest me, I wilwill do. IobJob 1. 5. And whēwhen the daiesdays of their bāquettingbanquetting were gone about, IobJob sent and sanctified them.
This obedience must shewshow it selfeself in two things.
First in the choycechoice of a lawfulllawful calling, wherein the child is to be ordered and appointed at the discretion of the parent.

Secondly in mariagemarriage: For in that, the parent is the principallprincipal agent and disposer of the child. Now although his authoritieauthority be not so great, as that the child is to be forced and compelled by him; yet the reuerentreverent and dutifulldutiful respect which the child ought to bearebear towards him, ought to be a strong inducement, not to dissent, or renounce his aduiceadvice, without great and waightieweighty cause. Yea the child must endeuourendeavour by all manner of dutifulldutiful cariagecarriage to ouercomeovercome, or at least to mitigate his parents seueritieseverity in that behalfebehalf.

Now for the daughters: They must yeeldyield obedience to their parents in all DomesticallDomestic labours, that they may be skilfullskilful in housholdhousehold affairesaffairs. Thus did the seuenseven daughters of the Priest of Midian, accustomeaccustom themseluesthemselves to draw water, and fill the troughestroughs to water
their fathers sheepesheep, Exod. 2. 16. Thus Rebekah was seeneseen to come out of her fathers house, with her pitcher vponupon her shoulder, and to go downedown with it to the well to fill it, and giuegive drinkedrink to her fathers Camels, Gen. 24. 16. 17.

The second dutieduty of the sonneson, is to recompencerecompense his fathers louelove, and care ouerover him, by relieuingrelieving him in case of want, if God giuegive abilitieability, with food and raymentraiment, and other necessaries. Herein children must dealedeal with their parents, as the brood of the StorkeStork is reported to do with her, by feeding her when she is old; wherein they doedo no more but what sheeshe before hath done vntounto them. It is Pauls counsellcounsel, that childredchildren & nephewesnephews should recompencerecompense the kindneskindness of their kindred in the first place, 1. Tim. 5. 4. andAnd therefore to their parents, the head & foūdationfoundation of their kindred. When IosephJoseph was in prosperitieprosperity, and his father IacobJacob in want, he first gauegave him cornecorn freely; and afterwards sent for him to Egypt, and there prouidedprovided for him; in so much as the text saith of him, that he nourished his father and
his brethren, and all his fathers house-hold with bread, EuenEven as the mother puts meat into the childs mouth, Gen. 47. 12. When Naomi the step-mother of Ruth was of great yearesyears, and her strength spent, Ruth gathered cornecorn in the haruestharvest for relieferelief of them both. Yea when Boaz gauegave her to eateeat and to drinkedrink, she reseruedreserved part of her victuals, & brought it home with her gleanesgleans to refresh her mother, Ruth 2. 14. 18.

The necessitienecessity of the performance of these duties is so great, that if the sonneson neglecteth them, and doth the contrariecontrary, by ill vsageusage of his parent, either in word or deed, he is worthieworthy of death, eueneven by Moses law: Exod. 21. 15. He that smiteth his father or his mother, shall die the death.

The law of the first borne of a mans children, that he should hauehave a greater portion of his fathers goods, then any of the rest of his brethren, is perpetuallperpetual, and admits no exception, but only in the case of notorious wickedneswickedness. Deut. 21. 17. He shall acknowledge the son of the hated for the first borne, & giuegive him a double
portion of all that he hath, for he is the first of his strength, and to him belongeth the right of the first borne. This was the law; yet we readeread that Ruben lost this prerogatiueprerogative, by reason of his incest, and IudahJudah the fourth sonneson of IacobJacob had the dignitiedignity of the first borne, Gen. 49. 8. Thou IudahJudah, thy brethren shall prayseprays thee—thy fathers sonnessons shall bow downedown vntounto thee.

In the Church of the old Testament, the priuiledgeprivilege of the first borne was three-fold; the first of gouernmentgovernment and royaltieroyalty, the second of Priesthood, the third of the double portion. And it is probable that this was for the most part CeremoniallCeremonial, and was accomplished and determined in Christ, who was the Imageimage of the inuisibleinvisible God, & the first borne of eueryevery creature, Colos. 1. 15.
HeereHere two questions are propounded.
Quest. I. Whether is it lawfulllawful for the sonneson to make a vow belonging either to religion, or to ciuillcivil conuersationconversation, without the consent of the parent?

Answ. A vow so made is not of force
to bind the child, but by the Law of nature & common equitieequity, is to be made void. For it is a ruled case, that he which is not his owneown man, that is to say, at his owneown libertieliberty, but vnderunder the power of another, cannot bind himselfehimself. AgaineAgain, the authoritieauthority of the parent by the law of God is great; For it alloweth the father to make void the vow of the child pertaining to Gods worship, Numb. 30. 6.
Quest. II. Whether is the consent of the parents to be required in the second mariagesmarriages of their children?

Answ. 1. Of ancient times, both by C. de Nuptijs. L. vidua, & L. in cōiunctioneconiunctione.CiuillCivil laweslaws, & also by Imperial constitutions, it was prouidedprovided that no widoweswidows, though made free by their former mariagesmarriages, should make any contract againeagain, without the good will of their parents. 2. Consent in this case, though it be not absolutely necessarienecessary, yet it is to be thought fit and conuenientconvenient, because children in some regards exempted from parents authoritieauthority, doedo owe notwithstanding the dutieduty of honor vntounto them, by Gods expresseexpress commandementcommandment,
Exod. 20. 12. andAnd consequently ought to testifietestify the same, by being ordered and aduisedadvised by them in some sort, eueneven at the after-bestowing of themseluesthemselves. Hence it is, thatBeza de repud. & diuort. sect. de spōsalibussponsalibus abs
que absque consensu parfactisparentum factis. later DiuinesDivines hauehave holden vponupon good ground; That the espousals of widoweswidows, who hauehave some more libertieliberty, then the child first married, being made without their parents knowledge, cannot but incurreincur iustjust reprehension, howsoeuerhowsoever they may stand in force without it.

div.head: CHAP. 15.
Of the Master.
div.p: NExtNext vntounto parents and children, wherbywhereby the family is increased, is a second sort of couples, which are helpeshelps theruntothereunto. And they are Mastersmasters and seruantsservants.
The Mastermaster is a member in the familiefamily, which hath power and beareth rule ouerover the seruantservant. And his dutieduty stands principally in three things.

First, To make a good choice of his seruantsservants; which is then done, when he inquireth first after such as fearefear God, and be willing to serueserve him. Paul makes the seruiceservice and fearefear of God the maine ground of true obedience in seruantsservants, Ephes. 6. 5. 6. 7. Colos. 3. 22. It was the rule of DauidsDavids choice, Psal. 101. 6. HeeHe that walketh in the perfect way, he shall serueserve me. Abrahams chiefechief seruātseruantservant of his house, was a man that feared God, as appeareth, in that he made conscience of his oath, Gen. 24. 2. 3. andAnd prayed also for successesuccess in the businesbusiness whereabout he was sent. Gen. 24. 12. O Lord God of my Mastermaster Abraham, I beseech thee send meeme good speed this day, and shewshow merciemercy to my Mastermaster Abraham. Cornelius of Caesarea, the CaptaineCaptain of the Italian band, had a souldiersoldier that daily attended on him, who feared God, and seruantsservants also beside him, to whom heehe made knowneknown the heauenlyheavenly vision which heehe saw, Act. 10. 7.

Secondly, To enioyneenjoin them labour, and not to require more of them, then their strength will bearebear. The master is
to rule ouerover the seruantservant in iusticejustice. And then is his cōmandementcommandementcommandment vniustunjust, whēwhen it will not stādstand with the course of nature, with the abilitieability of his seruantservant, or with the word of God. Therefore he is to require labour at their hādshands proportionable to their strength, & yeeldyield thēthem sometimes intercession & rest. LeuitLevit. 25. 46. OuerOver your brethenbrethren the children of Israel, ye shall not rule ouerover one another with crueltiecruelty. 1. Pet. 3. 8. BeeBe pitifullpitiful, beebe courteous, one bearebear with another. And for the furtherance of businesbusiness, it is conuenientconvenient that the master be oftentimes present with the seruātsseruantsservants in their works. ProuProv. 27. 23. Be diligent to know the state of thy flock, and take heed to thy heardsherds. The good matron ouerseethoverseeth the waiesways of her housholdhousehold, ProuProv. 31. 27.Arist. Oeconom. 7. A man of Libya being asked, what it was that might make a horse fat; he answered, The masters eye.
Thirdly, To recompencerecompense the diligence and painespains of his seruantservant, and that three waiesways.

First, by giuinggiving him his due of meat and drinkedrink for the present. The good matron giuethgiveth the portion to her housholdhousehold,
and the ordinary to her maids, ProuProv. 31. 15.

Secondly, by paying him his hire in the end of his seruiceservice: The labourer is worthieworthy of his wages. Luk. 10. 7. Well done, good seruantservant and faithfullfaithful; thou hast been faithfullfaithful in little, I will make thee ruler ouerover much; enter into thy masters ioyjoy. Mat. 25. 21.

HeereHere three caueatscaveats are to be obseruedobserved. I. That the wages be proportionable to the work. II. That it be paid in due time, without deferring. So the Mastermaster of the vine-yard, when eueneven was come, called his seruantsservants together, to giuegive thēthem their hire, Mat. 20. 8. III. That the seruātseruantservant be not defrauded of any part of his due. For this is a crying sin; Deut. 24. 15. Thou shalt giuegive him his hire for his day, neither shall the SunneSun go downedown vponupon it—lest heehe criecry against thee vntounto the Lord, and it beebe sinnesin vntounto thee. IamJam. 5. 4. Thirdly, if the seruantservant in time of his seruiceservice be sickesick, the masters care must
be by all means possible to procure his recoueryrecovery. EquitieEquity must be the rule in these cases; and masters are to do to their seruantsservants that which is iustjust and equallequal. Col. 4. 1. Now the seruantservant hapliehaply fallesfalls sickesick by and in his seruiceservice, and his health yeeldsyields not only profit to his master, but incouragementencouragement also to himselfehimself. The good Centurion in case of his seruantsservants sicknessesickness, tooketook the best course to hauehave him restored, Matth. 8. 6.

div.head: CHAP. 16.
Of the SeruantServant.
div.p: THeThe Seruantservant, is a person in the family subiectsubject vntounto his master.

The dutieduty of a seruātseruantservant is, faithfully and diligētlydiligently to demeanedemean himselfehimself in the affairesaffairs of his master, and to doedo seruiceservice vntounto him as vntounto Christ, though he be froward and hard-hartedhearted. Titus 2. 9. Let seruantsservants be subiectsubject to their masters, and please them in all things, not answering againeagain. Ephes. 6. 5. SeruantsServants, be
obedient to them that are your masters according to the flesh, with fearefear & trembling, in singlenessingleness of your hearts, as vntounto Christ. Col. 3. 22. Thus IacobJacob seruedserved Laban, Gen. 31. 38. This twentietwenty yearesyears hauehave I binbeen with thee; thine ewes and thy goatesgoats hauehave not cast their yongyoung, and the rammesrams of the flockeflock hauehave I not eaten, &c.

Contrariwise, the seruantservant must take heed that he doedo not his masters businessebusiness negligently, or for fashion sake, or with eye-seruiceservice as a man-pleaser; that in case of rebuke or controlementcontrolment, he answereanswer not againeagain; lastly, that heehe be trustietrusty & withhold his hands from picking, and his heart from deceiuingdeceiving his master.
SeruantsServants are of two sorts; either free, or bond-seruantsservants.

A free-seruantservant is he, whom his master hireth for wages to do him seruiceservice. To him belongs the iustjust paimentpayment of his hire, and in case of offence, them master hath authoritieauthority to censure and correct him, prouidedprovided that in the execution thereof, respect beebe had vntounto his age, and the correction be vsedused with moderation,
as if heehe were his sonneson.

A bond-seruantservant, is a seruantservant bought for money, and is commonly called a slaueslave. Touching this sort, a question is mouedmoved, whether a Christian may with safe conscience, hauehave and vseuse a man as his slaueslave?

Answ. The power & right of hauinghaving bond-men, in those countries where it is established by positiuepositive laweslaws, may stand with good cōscienceconscience, if it be vsedused with moderation. That authoritieauthority in this behalfebehalf is moderate, wherein these seuenseven caueatscaveats be obseruedobserved.

I. That the master hauehave not ouerover his seruantservant the power of life and death; for this takes away the lawful power of the Magistrate, to whom only the Lord hath committed the sword of iusticejustice.

II. That there be not libertieliberty granted him, to vseuse his seruantservant at his owneown will and pleasure in all things; for this was not granted by the law of God to his owneown people: Exod. 21. 26. If a man smite his seruantservant or his maid in the eye, and hath perished it, he shall let him go free for his eye: Also if he smite out his seruantsservants or
his maids tooth, he shall let him go out free for his tooth.
III. That the power be not enlarged to the commanding of things against piety or iusticejustice; for in these cases a man must rather obey God then man, Act. 4. 19.

IV. That masters do not take libertieliberty to make separation of those their seruantsservants that be married, the one from the other, or of those that be parents from their children; considering that God himselfehimself hath made these societies, and ioynedjoined such persons together, and therefore man may not separate them.

V. That the masters do not take libertieliberty to put ouerover their seruantsservants to vngodlyungodly and vnbelieuingunbelieving masters, for that is an vnkindunkind and cruellcruel libertieliberty, & may be an apparātapparantapparent occasion to make the seruantservant fall away from religion, and renounce the true God.

VI. That they do not bind them to perpetuallperpetual slaueryslavery, & neuernever make them free. Exo. 21. 5. But if the seruantservant say thus, I louelove my master, my wife and my children, I will not go out free.
VII. That the seruitudeservitude be not procured and retained by force; for it is a more grieuousgrievous crime to spoilespoil a man of his libertieliberty, then of his riches.
Now ytthat the same power limited with these cautions, is lawfulllawful & warrantable in cōsciēceconscience, it appears by these reasons.

I. God hath ordained & allowed it, eueneven by warrant of his owneown law: The posteritieposterity of Cham was cursed by Noah, and condemned to slauerieslavery, Gen. 9. 25. And he said, Cursed be Cham, a seruantservant of seruantsservants shalshall he be to his brethren. So were the Gibeonites by IoshuaJoshua, IosJos. 9. 23. Now therefore yeeye are cursed, and there shall none of you be freed from being bond-men, and hewers of wood, & drawers of water, for the house of my God. So was the theefethief, Exo. 22. 3. If he had not wherewith to make restitution, then heehe should beebe sold for his theft. Again, those that are ouercomeovercome in war may be held captiuecaptive, and it is lawful for the conquererconqueror to kill them, & therefore to make them slauesslaves: and if being takētaken, they be sauedsaved from death, they owe all that they hauehave to them by whom they are sauedsaved.

II. The law of God gauegave libertieliberty to any māman that would, to make sale of himselfehimself to another. LeuitLevit. 25. 45. Of the children of the strangers that are soiournerssojourners among you, of them shalshall ye buy, & of their families that are with you, which they begat in your land, these shall be your possessiōpossession. Deut. 15. 12. If thy brother an Hebrew sell himself to thee, or an HebrewesseHebrewess, and serueserve thee six yearesyears, euēeueneven in the seuenthseventh yeareyear thou shalt let him go free from thee: and vers. 17. Thou shalt take an auleawl, & pierce his eareear through against the dooredoor, and he shall be thy seruantservant for euerever.
III. The māman that is ransommedransomed frōfromfromfron his enemieenemy, is bound to serueserve as a slaueslave in liewlieu of thankfulnessethankfulness.

IV. The examples of the godly in the Scriptures. Abraham had seruantsservants whom he bought for siluersilver, Gen. 17. 12. EuerieEvery manchild of eight daiesdays old among you, shalshall be circumcised in your generations, as well he that is borne in thine house, as he that is bough with money of any stranger, which is not of thy seed. Gen. 24. 35. The Lord hath blessed my master Abraham wōderfullywonderfully— for he hath giuengiven him sheep and
beeuesbeeves, and siluersilver and gold, & men-seruantsservants and maid-seruantsservants, and camels and asses.

V. The Apostles do not disallow of such seruātsseruantsservants, but cōmandcommandcommandconmand thēthem being seruantsservants, & called to the professiōprofession of ChristianitieChristianity in that state, not to change, but to abide in their calling. 1. Cor. 7. 21. Art thou called being a seruantservant? careCare not for it.

It is alledgedalleged that such seruitudeservitude is against the law of nature. Ans. It is indeed against the law of intireentire nature, as it was before the fall, but against the law of corrupted nature since the fall, it is not.

But Christ hath purchased liberty to belieuersbelievers, Coloss. 5. 11. Ans. Only a spirituallspiritual libertieliberty in this life; & a corporal only in the life to come. For though y•y•the seruantservant in regard of faith & the inner man be equal to his master, because in Christ IesusJesus there is neither master nor seruātseruantservant, bond nor free; yet in regard of the outward man & ciuillcivil order amongst men, the master is aboueabove the seruantservant, and the seruantservant is, & must be subiectsubject to the master.Theodor▪. Orat. 8. NeuerthelesseNevertheless where this kind of seruitudeservitude is abolished, it is not to be againeagain receiuedreceived or intertainedentertained amongst
Christians, specially considering, it is a far more mildemild and moderate course to hauehave hired seruantsservants.

If it be said againeagain, that the Heathen Philosopher holdeth seruitudeservitude to be naturallnatural, wherbywhereby some are by birth bond, and others free. I answereanswer, That seruitudeservitude proceedeth not of nature,Aristot. polit. lib. 1. but hath his originalloriginal from the laweslaws of nations, and is a consequent of the fall. For all men by nature are equally & indifferētlyindifferently free, none more or lesseless then others.

div.head: CHAP. 17.
Of the Master of the familieFamilyfamily or goodmanGoodman of the houseHouse.
div.p: THusThus much touching the diuersdivers and seuerallseveral combinations or couples belonging to the state OeconomicallEconomical. The good man or master of the familiefamily, is a person, in whom resteth the priuateprivate and proper gouernmentgovernment of the whole
housholdhousehold, and he comes not vntounto it by election, as it falleth out in other states, but by the ordinance of God, setledsettled eueneven in the order of nature. The husbādhusband indeed naturally bearesbears rule ouerover the wife; parents ouerover their childrēchildren, masters ouerover their seruātsseruantsservants: but that person who by the prouidenceprovidence of God, hath yethe place of an husband, a father, a master in his house, the same also by the light of nature, hath the principality & soueraigntiesovereignty therein, and he is Paterfamilias, the father and chiefechief head of the familiefamily: to him therefore the true right and power ouerover all matters domestical, of right appertaineth. The duties of the master of the familiefamily, are specially fiuefive.

I. To bearebear the chiefechief stroke, and to be the principal agent, directerdirector and furtherer of the worship of God within his familiefamily. IosJos. 24. 15. I and my household wilwill serueserve the Lord. And this he doth partly by praying for & with his housholdhousehold, and partly by instructing thēthem in the holy Scriptures, and in the grounds of religiōreligion, that they may grow in knowledge and reapereap benefit by the publikepublic MinisterieMinistry.
Thus God commanded the men of Israel to walkewalk in their families. Deut. 6. 7. Thou shalt rehearse them continually vntounto thy children, and shalt talketalk of them, when thou tariest in thine house,—& when thou liest downedown, & when thou risest vpup. AgaineAgain, vers. 20. When thy sonneson shall askeask thee,—what meanemean these testimonies, and ordinācesordinances & laweslaws, which the Lord our God commanded you? Then thou shalt say vntounto thy son, We were Pharaohs bondmen in Egypt, but the Lord brought vsus out of Egypt, with a mightiemighty hand. This testimony God gauegave of Abraham before the law was giuengiven, Gen. 18. 19. For I know Abraham that he will command his sons, and his housholdhousehold after him, that they keepekeep the way of the Lord. And this housholdhousehold of Abraham was very large, for the holy Ghost saiessays long before, that he had three hundred and eighteeneeighteen, [Ethchanicau] suos initiatos. that were borne and brought vpup in his house, Gen. 14. 14.
